In this paper, we introduce Disaster Operational Response Agent benchmark (DORA), the first agentic benchmark for end-to-end disaster response: 515 expert-authored tasks across 45 real-world disaster events spanning 10 types, paired with expert-verified, replayable gold trajectories totaling 3,500 tool-call steps. Tasks span five dimensions that cover the operational disaster-response pipeline: disaster perception, spatial relational analysis, rescue and evacuation planning, temporal evolution reasoning, and multi-modal report synthesis. Agents compose calls from a 108-tool MCP library over heterogeneous geospatial data: optical, SAR, and multi-spectral imagery across single-, bi-, and multi-temporal sequences (0.015-10m GSD), complemented by elevation and social vector layers. We comprehensively evaluate 13 frontier LLMs on our benchmark, revealing three persistent challenges: 1) disaster-domain grounding exposes unique failure modes (damage-semantic grounding, sensor-modality mismatch, and disaster-pipeline composition); 2) agents are doubly bottlenecked by tool selection and argument grounding, where gold tool-order hints improve accuracy by only 1.08-4.40%, and alternative scaffolds yield at most a 3.24% gain; 3) compositional fragility scales with trajectory length, the agent-to-gold gap widening from 7% to 56% on long pipelines. DORA establishes a rigorous testbed for operationally reliable disaster-response agents. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Junjue-Wang/DORA.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Action-Aligned Latent Planning for Versatile Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Yutang Lin, Guanya Shi, C. Karen Liu
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The FIBER framework enables versatile humanoid loco-manipulation by integrating high-level planning with low-level control through a shared latent space, achieving significant performance improvements in diverse tasks.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Learning a single perceptive policy for diverse humanoid loco-manipulation requires unifying high-level task decisions without losing the state-dependent physical responses that make each interaction succeed. This makes the representation between high-level planning and whole-body control critical: kinematic or contact targets provide compact abstractions but do not directly encode interaction-specific control responses, while directly predicting low-level actions requires the planner to model high-frequency closed-loop feedback. We propose FIBER, a framework that uses the executable latent space of a frozen behavioral foundation model (BFM) as a shared planning representation for heterogeneous interaction skills. Our latent policy projection (LPP) maps independently acquired task-specific policies into this representation by identifying latent commands whose induced actions match their local control responses, enabling lower-rate planning while retaining the BFM's high-frequency state feedback. After projection, we aggregate closed-loop latent rollouts from all skills and train a single perceptive flow planner entirely offline. We further introduce AH-BFM, an adaptive-horizon BFM trained with multi-gamma forward-backward (FB) learning to support both precise control and temporally extended whole-body behavior. We evaluate FIBER on box pickup, door opening, and object grasping in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Across 128 diverse variations per task in simulation, FIBER achieves 42.0% mean success, more than tripling projected latent replay (11.6%) and substantially outperforming kinematic planning (3.5%). Real-world experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering through the same unified planner.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Dream What I Can: Sparse Visual Planning for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Chongkai Gao, Wenlong Huang, Haonan Chen, Lin Shao, Yilun Du
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: DreamCan introduces a hierarchical policy for robot manipulation that utilizes sparse visual planning to generate executable subgoals from video models, outperforming existing planning methods.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Video models provide rich priors for generalizable robotic manipulation, but plausible visual futures are not always executable. We introduce DreamCan, a hierarchical policy that grounds video models through sparse visual planning: a high-level planner adapted from a pre-trained video model and a low-level visuomotor policy. Rather than predicting dense trajectories, the high-level planner generates sparse visual subgoals that balance reachability and task utility. From offline, action-free robot videos, we estimate these quantities and use dynamic programming to select subgoal sequences without manual annotations. The resulting subgoals are more reliably attained than uniformly spaced alternatives, and the full system outperforms language, dense-video, and uniform-subgoal planners, reaching high planning success rates on Language-Table tasks and 91.2% success on LIBERO-Long with a 0.1B-parameter low-level policy. Additional suboptimal videos and test-time compute further improve success. The system also performs challenging real-world bimanual tasks, including box folding and packing with unseen object combinations. More results are available at https://dreamcan.github.io/.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Test-Time Hinting for Black-Box Vision-Language Models
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Kaihua Hou, Abhijith Varma Mudunuri, Jiaxing Qiu, Roxana Daneshjou, Thomas Hartvigsen
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: This paper introduces Test-Time Hinting, a method enhancing black-box vision-language model performance by providing targeted hints to mitigate common error patterns without model access.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) methods have proven highly effective for LLMs, yet their application to vision-language models (VLMs) remains relatively underexplored. Existing VLM TTS methods largely require open-weight model access or expensive repeated sampling, and are evaluated primarily on multimodal mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks rather than natural-image understanding. In this paper, we propose Test-Time Hinting, a method that improves VLM performance with a single call to the target VLM and requires only black-box API access, which makes it broadly applicable to frontier closed-weight models. Our method is motivated by the observation that VLM errors tend to cluster around recurring failure patterns that are shared across models and predictable from the input alone. We therefore train a lightweight hint generator model to predict, for a given test input, which "hint" should be prepended to the prompt, providing targeted contextual or procedural guidance that steers the VLM away from its characteristic failure modes without revealing the answer. We show that Test-Time Hinting significantly improves the accuracy of multiple closed-weight VLMs on natural-image VQA benchmarks and that these gains generalize to unseen benchmarks and VLMs without retraining the hint generator.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: SteerAct: Unlocking Action Models through Few-Shot Temporal Steering
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Kaichen Zhou, Zhiyan Li, Chongkai Gao, Yuhan Wang, Wenlong Huang
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: SteerAct enhances pretrained robot action models by using few-shot temporal steering to optimize feature activations, improving task success by 10% without weight updates.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Improving pretrained robot action models at test time from only a few rollouts remains challenging. Activation steering offers a lightweight approach by modifying feature activations while keeping model weights fixed. However, effective steering requires identifying which features to modify and determining the timing and strength of modification. We introduce SteerAct, a few-shot temporal steering framework that uses a shared temporal descriptor of sparse-feature dynamics for offline feature selection and online control. A pretrained sparse autoencoder provides candidate features, and our temporal descriptor summarizes the distribution of local activation-order patterns for each feature, enabling comparisons across rollouts without requiring timestep alignment. Before steering begins (offline), we use successful and failed reference rollouts to select a single task-specific feature whose temporal descriptors best distinguish the two outcomes and construct its reference banks. During each new execution (online), we compare the feature's evolving temporal descriptor with these references to determine when to intervene and how strongly to increase or decrease its activation via a steering coefficient. Using only 24 outcome-labeled rollouts per task, SteerAct improves task success by approximately 10% relative to unsteered models in evaluations spanning $π_{0.5}$, Fast-WAM, RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and real-world manipulation, without updating action-model weights. Code and demos are available at: https://steeract.github.io/.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Long-Horizon Multi-Object Rearrangement via Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Kallol Saha, Yining Hong, Amber Li, Yejin Choi, Maxim Likhachev
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: DISCO introduces a method for long-horizon multi-object rearrangement by combining distilled tree search with continuous action policies, outperforming traditional approaches in both simulation and real-world tasks.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Despite recent advances in policy learning, long-horizon manipulation remains difficult because learned policies must avoid compounding errors while preserving future feasibility. While search-based planning can explicitly reason over such future consequences, it quickly becomes expensive in high-dimensional continuous action spaces. This raises a central question: how can long-horizon reasoning from search be transferred into policies in continuous action spaces? To this end, we propose DISCO: Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions. DISCO uses progressive-widening MCTS in physics simulation to generate long-horizon plans. During search, a learned policy proposes continuous actions, while a learned value function scores actions by their expected progress toward task completion. Using GPU-parallelized simulation, DISCO periodically distills MCTS-generated plans into the policy-value model, improving the action proposals and value estimates used in subsequent searches. Finally, the learned policy-value model can be directly deployed without the need for simulator-based search at test time. Across simulated and real-world rearrangement tasks, DISCO outperforms behavior cloning, reinforcement learning, and search-based baselines.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Self-Supervised Inertial Odometry
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Yuheng Qiu, Yutian Chen, Carlton Cort, Weison Huang, Shibo Zhao
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The paper presents a self-supervised method for training inertial odometry models without ground-truth trajectories, achieving high accuracy through myopic integration and pose graph distillation.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Learning inertial odometry for a new platform usually requires ground-truth trajectories. We show that an inertial odometry model can instead be trained from scratch by a myopic teacher that integrates the IMU over each short window independently, a scheme we call integration self-supervision.Interestingly, although supervised only by short-window velocity changes, the student learns to directly predict velocity, and does so more accurately than its integration teacher. Pose graph distillation then refines the model with sequence-consistent targets from a pose graph over many windows. Training on a new platform therefore no longer requires collecting ground-truth trajectories, but only calibrating the IMU and recording data during normal operation. Across six datasets spanning pedestrians, drones, quadrupeds, and a humanoid, the same recipe with no velocity or position labels trains models that come within $0.07$~m/s average velocity error of a same-architecture supervised baseline.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Computational Multi-Agents Society Experiments: Social Modeling Framework Based on Generative Agents
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Hanzhong Zhang, Muhua Huang, Jindong Wang
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: CMASE is a generative agent-based framework enabling in-world researcher participation and traceable interventions for enhanced social modeling and intervention studies.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Computational social science has developed descriptive, interpretative, and predictive modeling, but comprehensive modeling combining in-world human intervention with outcome forecasting remains underexplored. Generative agent-based platforms scale populations or reproduce complex scenarios, but researchers typically act through setup, external controls, or post-hoc analysis rather than in-world roles. We introduce Computational Multi-Agent Society Experiments (CMASE), a generative agent-based framework for in-world researcher participation and traceable interventions at runtime. Treating simulation as a simulated ethnographic field, CMASE supports (1) real-time human-computer interaction to study intervention processes; (2) controlled experiments with ethnography-inspired observation, interviewing, and interpretation; and (3) forward exploration of intervention trajectories and downstream responses. CMASE combines LLM-driven perception, memory, and emotion; a composable environment built from texture and area maps; and researcher roles spanning observation, interviewing, participation, and intervention, so that interventions enter as social events rather than exogenous parameters. We replicate two published field studies from different disciplines: urban greenery and social fragmentation, and cooperation in a public goods game, using two substantially different language models. CMASE reproduces reported statistical patterns and provides process-level records for mechanism-oriented interpretation. A controlled comparison shows that embedded social interventions leave observable, auditable processes that parametric manipulation does not. These findings highlight CMASE's methodological value for studying interventions in small- and medium-scale social settings and its interdisciplinary potential. The official code is available at: https://github.com/armihia/CMASE.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Demystifying When and Why VLAs Fail in Contact-Rich Tasks and How to Fix Them
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Carlota Parés-Morlans, Nils Kuhn, Y. Isabel Liu, Alberta Longhini, Jeannette Bohg
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The paper identifies two failure modes in Vision-Language-Action models for contact-rich tasks and introduces FACT, improving success rates from 41% to 66% through enhanced action prediction and force conditioning.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: We address the problem of understanding when and why Vision-Language-Action models struggle with contact-rich manipulation tasks that require precise physical interaction. Prior work has primarily focused on addressing contact failures through force-augmented architectures and training-time regularizers, yet the factors contributing to these failures remain underexplored. We identify two distinct failure modes underlying this gap. Precision failures occur when policies struggle to produce the small, accurate corrective actions required during contact and force failures occur when policies fail to respond to contact forces. To address these failures, we propose FACT. During post-training, FACT increases low noise sampling to improve fine action prediction and incorporates structured force conditioning to guide action generation using contact state and force history. FACT achieves an average success rate of 66% across five contact-rich tasks against 41% for the best prior baseline, in an evaluation spanning almost 2,500 real-world rollouts.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Scaling Online Exploration for Robot Agents
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Runhan Huang, Xiangcheng Zhang, Haoyu Chen, Yitong Li, Yen-Jen Wang
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: RAX is an open-source framework that enhances robot agents' online exploration capabilities, enabling autonomous skill acquisition and improved generalization across diverse tasks without prior demonstration data.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Robot learning has advanced by scaling demonstration datasets and model capacity; however, deploying a new robot embodiment or task typically necessitates a dedicated teleoperation corpus. The resulting policies remain bounded by their imitation distributions, limiting generalization and continual self-improvement. We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), an open-source framework for robot agents centered on scaling exploration: enabling agents to improve by acquiring online experience and synthesizing executable programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent generates robot control code, operating without action demonstration data, hand-engineered action primitives, or value-function guidance. Through online exploration, the agent identifies decision sequences that achieve task goals and compiles them into modular programs encapsulating the full perception-planning-control loop. Using RAX, we present a systematic multi-embodiment study on scaling online exploration across precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks using single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid systems in simulation and on real robots. Generalization performance on unseen environments improves consistently as exploration scales. In simulation, RAX outperforms top baseline models by +37.4% on average. On real robots, RAX autonomously learns memory-dependent, articulated, high-precision, deformable, and long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks without human demonstrations, continually improving performance by composing verified skills from prior exploration sessions. As exploration scales, we observe emergent capabilities including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and human-robot collaboration. We open-source RAX as a generalist robot-agent platform in which new robot embodiments are integrated through their APIs alone, without teleoperated data collection or policy training.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Generative Policy Improvement from Observational Data
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Jonas Schweisthal, Dennis Frauen, Stefan Feuerriegel, Emma Brunskill
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The paper presents PolicyLift, a three-stage framework for improving decision policies from observational data, effectively addressing challenges in generating structured actions like text and images.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: We study how to improve decision policies from observational data to generate better actions when actions are complex, structured objects, such as text messages or images. This task is subject to two major challenges: (i) action-level overlap is often too weak for reliable off-policy evaluation and improvement, and (ii) generating new structured actions often requires expensive training or fine-tuning (e.g., of an LLM) and can be ill-defined due to information loss in action representations. To address both, we propose PolicyLift, a three-stage framework for generative policy improvement with structured actions from observational data. In Stage 1, PolicyLift learns a small set of discrete action codes that capture high-level strategies in the observed action space and are tailored to support policy improvement under limited overlap. In Stage 2, it learns a context-dependent policy over these action codes. At deployment time, Stage 3 "lifts" the learned code-level policy back to the original action space by generating actions from the historical behavior system in a code-conditioned way. We show theoretically that improving the policy over action codes guarantees improvement of the induced policy in the original action space. We demonstrate PolicyLift across experiments in synthetic and real-world text generation tasks with consistent policy improvements over the behavior policy.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Adibvafa Fallahpour, Parsa Idehpour, Vignesh Kothapalli, Nikita Mounier, Shirley Wu
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: Memorilla enhances frozen LLMs by efficiently encoding and retrieving query-specific information from extensive document collections using a limited number of memory tokens, improving performance in various tasks.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Memory enables large language models (LLMs) to use information beyond their parameters, such as past user conversations, long documents, or an agent's earlier actions. For a frozen LLM, access to this accumulated knowledge is limited to what a memory system places in its context window. However, gathering and combining relevant information needed for each query while keeping the model's context short remains challenging for existing systems. Here we introduce Memorilla, a memory system that gathers information from an entire document collection into a fixed number of query-dependent 'memory tokens' for a frozen LLM. Memorilla encodes documents (such as user chats, book chapters) once into reusable embeddings, then learns to retrieve and place query-specific information in the LLM's input embedding space. Using only 16 memory tokens, Memorilla achieves the best performance against baselines including Mem0 and MemoRAG on five of eight benchmarks spanning personalization, long-document and knowledge-intensive question answering. Notably, on FactKG, it reaches 84.33% accuracy versus 80.43% with full-context inference, while using 108x fewer tokens to represent the source documents. Furthermore, Memorilla can facilitate continual learning in agentic systems where the document count (the agent's past turns) increases throughout the trajectory. In a TextWorld environment, we show that Memorilla reduces the agent's tendency to wander between rooms it has already explored, and improves its average success rate from 18.6% with full-history in-context learning to 24.2%. Overall, Memorilla aids frozen LLMs in accumulating and using knowledge effectively across long-context interactions and takes a step towards building continually learning AI systems.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: World Modeling through Spectral Alignment
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Holger Molin, William Peng, Marco Bagatella, Randall Balestriero
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The paper introduces SpecWM, a framework for world modeling that uses spectral representation learning to enhance latent space control and improve planning success through targeted similarity kernels.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: How do we tell a world model what information to preserve? We study this question through the lens of spectral representation learning. We introduce SpecWM, a JEPA framework that explicitly specifies desired relationships between observations through a target similarity kernel and trains the encoder to reproduce those relationships in its embedding geometry. Different kernels provide different supervision, ranging from physical state information to a fully self-supervised temporal kernel requiring only the ordering of observations within trajectories. We characterize the global optima of the objective, establish conditions for linear recoverability and invariance to nuisance information, and connect temporal-kernel similarity to the behavioral successor measure under an idealized setting. Empirically, the choice of kernel strongly controls which physical quantities are recoverable from the representation. More importantly, temporal spectral alignment improves CEM planning success over LeWorldModel from 52% to 68% on OGBench Cube, 49% to 77% on OGBench Scene, and 29% to 51% on CALVIN. These results suggest that explicitly specifying representation geometry provides a simple way to steer what latent world models preserve for control.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Causal Analysis of Robot Foundation Models Enables Efficiency Gains
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Mozes Jacobs, Siddharth Boppana, Tal Haklay
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: This paper analyzes causal pathways in vision-language-action models, revealing efficiency gains by optimizing action expert conditioning, reducing inference costs without sacrificing performance.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are a promising approach to general purpose robot manipulation. While the internal computation of vision-language models, which compose the backbone of VLAs, has been studied extensively, less is known about how their perceptual and semantic representations are transformed into action in VLA models. We study this question mechanistically in three frontier VLA models ($π_{0.5}$, MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot) by analyzing the causal pathways through which the input image and the instruction shape actions. Across the three models, activation patching shows that causally relevant information influences the action expert (AE) through a narrow band of mid-to-late cross-attention layers, which we term the action-conditioning interface. The content of this information changes with token and layer within the model. Early-to-mid layer representations of the target noun token determine which object is selected, whereas mid-to-late layers carry the spatial information in text tokens that redirects the movement when patched. Where spatial information is stored in prompt tokens various based on the architecture. In MolmoAct2 the model forms task-conditioned representations at the text positions that follow the instruction, whereas $π_{0.5}$ additionally stores this information at image token positions. We show that these findings can be translated directly into improving model efficiency. We find that restricting MolmoBot's action expert conditioning to only 3 out of 36 layers reduces inference FLOPs by up to $33\%$ while maintaining comparable task success with the default model across 3,000 evaluation episodes ($46.7\%$ vs. $46.9\%$), and the same principle carries over to real-robot deployment of $π_{0.5}$.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Multi-Dimensional Featurizers Yield Fine-Grained Steering and Data Shaping in Robot Foundation Models
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Aiden Swann, Mozes Jacobs, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, David Chanin
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: This paper demonstrates that block-sparse featurizers enhance robot behavior control by enabling interpretable steering and data shaping through multi-dimensional feature recovery.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Can better feature discovery improve control over robot behavior through internal interventions and training data? Recent work in vision and language models reveals multidimensional features, motivating block-sparse featurizers (BSFs), which represent each feature in a low-dimensional subspace. We investigate whether recovering this structure provides an interpretable interface for steering vision-language-action models and shaping the data from which they learn. We show that BSFs recover several multi-dimensional task-relevant features underlying the model's computation (e.g., perception, language, proprioceptive state, episode phase, and control variables). We causally validate these features through fine-grained steering: targeted changes in visual perception, semantic representation, and spatial localization produce predictable changes in downstream action prediction. Finally, we use feature-based data attribution to isolate where a specific behavior (failure recovery) arises in the training dataset, identifying fewer than $1.4\%$ of training tokens whose masking is sufficient to remove the targeted behavior. Overall, our results show how matching featurizers to representation geometry can provide more effective tools for understanding and changing robot behavior.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Play2Perfect: What Matters in Dexterous Play Pretraining for Precise Assembly?
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Tyler Ga Wei Lum, Kushal Kedia, C. Karen Liu, Jeannette Bohg
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The Play2Perfect framework enhances robotic assembly by pretraining through diverse play, achieving significant efficiency and success in precise manipulation tasks.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Multi-fingered robots promise the speed and dexterity of human hands, yet challenging problems such as precise assembly have remained out of reach. These tasks are contact-rich, making data collection for imitation learning difficult, and sparse-reward, making direct exploration with reinforcement learning (RL) intractable. Consequently, prior work has made progress by structuring the problem with specialized grippers, tool attachments, and environment fixtures. In this work, we argue that before a robot can perfect precise assembly, it must first learn to play. We further ask the question: what factors in the process of learning to play matter for precise assembly? We propose Play2Perfect, an RL framework for task-agnostic pretraining through play on diverse objects and goals, which is then perfected on precise assembly. The goal of play is to acquire reusable manipulation priors, such as grasping, in-hand reorientation and pose reaching. Finetuning then adapts this general prior to assembly, focusing exploration on the final contact-rich, high-precision interactions needed for success. We systematically study key design choices in play pretraining, including object diversity, training objective, trajectory diversity, and goal precision. We show that our prior is 33x more sample-efficient than RL training from scratch, even when provided with dense, multi-stage rewards. We demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, achieving 60% success on tight insertions with only 0.5 mm contact clearance, and over 50% success on long-horizon multi-part assembly and screwing.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Bridging the Markerless Tracking Validation Gap: Intraoperative X-ray Workflow Integration
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Connor Daly, Salvatore Russo, Jinendra Ekanayake, Daniel S. Elson, Ferdinando Rodriguez y Baena
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: This paper presents a novel pipeline integrating intraoperative X-ray with RGB-D sensors for accurate validation of markerless spinal tracking, establishing a reliable ground truth for clinical applications.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Markerless intraoperative tracking of spinal anatomy via RGB-D sensors is a promising alternative to invasive bone-anchored fiducials, yet no existing clinical dataset provides independent subsurface ground truth for validating these methods. We address this gap with a clinically viable pipeline that derives per-vertebra 6-DoF pose from routine intraoperative C-arm fluoroscopy, co-registered to the RGB-D camera frame through a multimodal fiducial array detectable in both imaging modalities. Critically, the pipeline requires no additional radiation, instrumentation, or deviation from standard surgical workflows, relying solely on the fluoroscopic images already acquired during routine level checks. A calibrated transform chain links the vertebral pose recovered via multi-view 2D-3D CT-to-fluoroscopy registration to the RGB-D coordinate frame, enabling direct comparison of any markerless registration estimate against a subsurface reference. Ex vivo validation against optically tracked ovine vertebrae confirms end-to-end accuracy of 2.06 +- 0.29 mm and 3.35 +- 0.93 degrees, sufficient to serve as independent ground truth for methods with substantially larger errors. We demonstrate the pipeline's utility by evaluating two markerless registration strategies on clinical data spanning 11 vertebrae across 1,500 frames from three surgical sequences: the first such evaluation against an independent subsurface reference in a clinical setting. The proposed framework provides reusable infrastructure for benchmarking emerging markerless tracking methods on real surgical data.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Safe and Fuel-Efficient Motion Planning for Lunar Propulsive Drones
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Elena Wittemyer, Graco Gao
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: This paper presents an autonomous motion planning framework for lunar drones that ensures safe, fuel-efficient hops using vision-guided control and obstacle detection.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Propulsive drones are a promising new technology for generating high-resolution terrain models of the Moon. In future lunar missions, propulsive drones will complete a series of hops across the lunar surface while capturing images with downward-facing cameras. We present an autonomous motion planning framework that uses a vision-guided optimal control strategy for performing safe, efficient hops between specified waypoints. The drone plans parabolic hops between waypoints generated by a global-level planner; if a nominal waypoint is unsafe or unreachable, the drone then completes a diversion maneuver to safely land. To evaluate the validity of potential landing sites, we develop a custom semantic segmentation model for identifying obstacles from aerial images, and we introduce an approach for rapidly calculating reachable terrain. We then use model predictive control (MPC) to robustly track hop trajectories that guide the drone towards safe landing sites. We test the optimal hop planner in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. Our results demonstrate that our unified motion planning framework yields safe, fuel-efficient hop trajectories which can be tracked rapidly and with low error via MPC.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Anikait Singh, Teresa Zhang, Yoonho Lee, Roshen Sanjay Nair, Aviral Kumar
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: Librarian Agents enhance LLMs by proactively organizing unstructured data into tailored workspaces, improving query response accuracy and efficiency through reinforcement learning.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Reasoning over long document contexts remains a challenge for large language models (LLMs). Standard retrieval methods are inherently reactive, bottlenecking agents with complex, cross-document reasoning at inference time, while precomputed structures like knowledge graphs often fall short because they rely on rigid heuristics. Instead, can we allow agents to perform anticipatory directed curation: learning to proactively reorganize unstructured corpora prior to inference to efficiently serve diverse future queries. We build on a key asymmetry in modern agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code): while LLM agents are adept at navigating existing filesystems to solve an immediate task, they are rarely trained to construct reusable workspaces for future use. To instantiate this capability, we introduce Librarian Agents, a framework in which a builder agent transforms raw documents into a hierarchical filesystem of synthetic files and reference links, which forms a workspace tailored for a downstream answering agent. We formulate workspace construction as a Markov decision process and optimize the builder policy via reinforcement learning to directly maximize downstream answering accuracy. Empirically, Librarian Agents outperforms the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines by 33 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus, amortizes upfront construction costs across repeated queries, and generalizes zero-shot to unseen domains on BRIGHT with a 31-point average accuracy improvement.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: T2-z: Test-Time Optimization of Environment Latents for Robotic World Models
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Chenyuan Zhou, Yining Hong, Huang Huang, Yunfan Jiang, Wenlong Huang
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: T2-Z optimizes environment latents at test time, enhancing robotic world models to improve predictions and action success in diverse settings without prior environmental knowledge.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules. We introduce T2-Z for test-time optimization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact latent captures underlying environmental variation without supervision of what environmental factors exist or what values they take. During training, T2-Z alternates between two stages: a world-model optimization stage that fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments; and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction. At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-Z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. Its emergent latents capture structured representations of individual and compounded factors across diverse visual scenes. Ablations further show that T2-Z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Mozes Jacobs, Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, Fenil R. Doshi
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: This paper explores the multi-dimensional geometric representations of task-relevant concepts in vision-language-action models, revealing their significance in robotic manipulation beyond mere readability.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it? Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional. Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts in VLA models. We find that realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and is shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts. Physical joint limits, for example, leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, is realized in two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp. The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, indicating that they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation. We demonstrate how the findings are actionable by steering along the geometry a concept realizes. Overall, this work lays out an initial phenomenology of realized geometry in VLA policies and demonstrates that a concept's shape carries as much importance as its readability.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: The Invisible Leash: Why RLVR May or May Not Escape Its Origin
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Fang Wu, Weihao Xuan, Danny Xing, Ximing Lu, Mingjie Liu
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The paper critiques Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), revealing it may enhance reliability of known outputs while limiting access to diverse verified solutions.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Recent advances highlight Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) as a promising approach to enhancing LLM capabilities. However, it remains unclear whether the current practice of RLVR truly expands models' reasoning boundary or mainly amplifies high-reward outputs that base models already know. We introduce empirical support dynamics, a framework that quantifies how RLVR preserves, expands, and shrinks access to verified solutions. Applied across models, reasoning tasks, and training checkpoints, it matches verified successes question by question to reveal changes that aggregate accuracy can conceal. Across the evaluated model-level benchmark aggregates, \textit{the shrinkage of observed support outweighs its expansion}: more questions lose a verified success than gain one at the stated sampling budgets. These losses occur alongside gains in \texttt{pass@1}. Some RLVR models increase average token-level entropy while reducing final-answer entropy: their token choices become more uncertain on average even as their final answers become more concentrated. Together, these findings reveal an ``invisible leash'' in current RLVR practice: it can make existing successes more reliable while losing access to other verified solutions. Empirical support dynamics make this imbalance measurable and motivate exploration strategies that reach underrepresented solutions while retaining prior successes.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Constrained Whole-Body Tracking for Humanoid Robots
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Daniel Morton, Pranit Mohnot, Marco Pavone
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The paper presents ConstrainedMimic, a control framework that ensures real-time constraint enforcement in humanoid robot motion tracking using reinforcement learning, enhancing safety and agility.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) have demonstrated impressive whole-body agility for humanoid robots, yet ensuring safety and satisfying constraints -- particularly those specified after training -- remains a challenge. Towards this goal, we present ConstrainedMimic, a control framework that leverages whole-body kinematics and dynamics for real-time constraint enforcement within RL tracking policies. By integrating principles from operational space control and control barrier functions, we enable the satisfaction of arbitrary runtime constraints on both the kinematic reference motion and the underlying dynamics, with efficient computation at frequencies above 1 kHz. In whole-body motion-tracking experiments in simulation and hardware, we demonstrate collision avoidance (both with the robot body and external obstacles), joint limits, and center of mass stability constraints. By remaining consistent with the current contact mode and tracking objectives, we minimally restrict the capabilities of the policy when constraints are active. Project page: https://stanfordasl.github.io/constrainedmimic.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: LEGS: Fine-Tuning Teleop-Free VLAs for Humanoid Loco-manipulation in an Embodied Gaussian Splatting World
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Hojune Kim, Timothy Chen, Jiankai Sun, Lars W. Osterberg, Qianzhong Chen
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: LEGS introduces a hybrid simulator for humanoid loco-manipulation, enabling scalable, teleoperation-free training of vision-language-action policies that outperform traditional methods.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies for humanoid loco-manipulation is constrained by the high cost and complexity of collecting human teleoperation demonstrations. VLA policies fine-tuned in simulators have so far transferred poorly to humanoid loco-manipulation tasks. We present LEGS (Loco-manipulation via Embodied Gaussian Splatting), a hybrid simulator that composites a mesh foreground (robot, objects, props) over a photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) background reconstructed from a handheld scene capture. LEGS uses a procedural motion-primitive generator to synthesize labeled demonstrations at scale without human teleoperation, and a two-stage color calibration that aligns renders to the deployment camera. On a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, across three pick-and-place tasks of increasing whole-body difficulty and three VLA backbones ($ψ_0$, $π_{0.5}$, GR00T N1.6), a policy trained purely on LEGS data matches or exceeds one trained on human teleoperation demos on every experiment. It also outperforms a mesh-only baseline trained on the same motions without the calibrated 3DGS frontend. Because motion is recorded independently of appearance, the same demonstrations can be re-rendered for a target scene and objects at over 15x lower cost than teleoperation. When both the objects and the scene change, a policy trained on LEGS-AUG data re-rendered for that target maintains task success, while the teleop baseline fails entirely. Code and videos are available at https://hojjunekim.github.io/legs/.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: DIRECT: When and Where Should You Allocate Test-Time Compute in Embodied Planners?
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Jadelynn Dao, Milan Ganai, Yasmina Abukhadra, Ajay Sridhar, Mozhgan Nasr Azadani
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The DIRECT framework optimizes test-time compute allocation in embodied planners, enhancing performance while reducing latency and resource usage compared to traditional scaling methods.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as high-level planners for embodied agents, with an emerging strategy of scaling test-time compute to improve capability. However, we observe that doing so increases latency, token usage, and FLOPs while yielding uneven, often diminishing gains in downstream success, limiting where embodied agents can be deployed. We argue that choosing when and where to spend test-time compute is central to bringing frontier performance to the real world, and we can budget inference at the planning level. We introduce DIRECT, a routing framework that uses multimodal scene context to allocate compute at each step of a closed-loop agent, selecting a planner for every subtask, improving the success--cost Pareto frontier over fixed model selection. Across three dominant scaling axes, namely chain-of-thought depth, model size, and memory history, our experiments on VLABench and RoboMME show that test-time compute is not a uniform lever: different axes yield qualitatively distinct capability gains. We validate these insights on a physical Franka arm in a DROID setup spanning zero-shot manipulation and long-horizon chaining, where our router matches or exceeds a stronger model's success rate at up to 65% lower average latency. Ultimately, our results show that naively scaling test-time compute is wasteful, and DIRECT can provide frontier-level embodied planning at a fraction of the cost. Project page can be found at jadee-dao.github.io/direct/.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: TrAct: Bridging Robot Control and Visual Prediction with Visual Tracks
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Zhi Cao, Howard Ji, Kevin Zhang, Kuangzhi Ge, Li Fei-Fei
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: TrAct enhances robot decision-making by using visual tracks as an embodiment-agnostic interface, improving action prediction and task success rates in simulations and real-world scenarios.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Robot actions are inherently embodiment-specific and only weakly aligned with image-space visual changes, limiting their effectiveness as conditioning signals for robot world models. In contrast, visual tracks provide an embodiment-agnostic representation of how task-relevant points move through a scene, offering dense image-space guidance for accurate and spatially precise future video prediction. Building on this observation, we propose TrAct, a world-model-based robot decision-making framework that uses visual tracks as an intermediate interface between control and prediction. TrAct consists of three components: a Vision-Language-Action-and-Track model (VLAT) that jointly predicts candidate actions and corresponding visual tracks from the current observation and language instruction; a track-conditioned world model (TWM) that predicts future visual outcomes conditioned on the proposed tracks; and a vision-language reward model (VLAC) that scores the predicted outcomes. At inference time, VLAT generates candidate action-track pairs, TWM rolls out their visual consequences, and VLAC selects the track whose predicted outcome best satisfies the instruction; the action paired with the selected track is then executed by the robot. Experiments on the proposed LIBERO-INTEGRAL benchmark and real-world Franka manipulation show that TrAct improves success rates from 27% to 55% in simulation and from 49% to 76% on real-world tasks compared with the strong VLA baseline $π_{0.5}$. Furthermore, TWM consistently improves video prediction quality over the action-conditioned world model (AWM). These results demonstrate that visual tracks provide an effective shared interface between robot control and visual prediction, enabling more accurate world modeling and stronger robot generalization.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: FACT: A Multimodal Force-Action-Track Foundation Model for Human-to-Robot Dexterity
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Zhi Cao, Yining Hong, Jiaolong Yang, Yejin Choi, Li Fei-Fei
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The FACT model integrates a large-scale human tactile dataset with robot demonstrations to enhance dexterous manipulation through force-aware planning and refinement, achieving significant performance improvements.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative to costly robot data collection for dexterous manipulation, but most human datasets lack force measurements. Dexterous manipulation requires not only visual and proprioceptive understanding but also the ability to anticipate and regulate interaction forces. To scale force-aware human-robot co-training, we introduce EgoForce, a large-scale human tactile dataset capturing force-rich manipulation experience, and combine it with robot demonstrations for pretraining. We present FACT, a robot foundation model that cascades from prospective visual planning to force-aware refinement for dexterous manipulation. FACT comprises two jointly trained components. A Track-Guided Coarse Planner jointly predicts actions, future video, and visual tracks. Future video and visual tracks also provide a shared task representation that facilitates cross-embodiment knowledge transfer and coarse action generation. Building on this coarse plan, a Force-Action Joint Refiner jointly predicts future force and refines the coarse action, allowing anticipated force and action to shape each other during refinement. We evaluate the model on ten tasks requiring fine-grained coordination and force feedback, including tool use, musical instruments, and precision laboratory procedures. Using as few as 10 robot trajectories with 90 human trajectories for fine-tuning, FACT outperforms both baselines, with success-rate gains of up to 60 percentage points over T-Rex. Ablations show that force supervision in human pretraining data is crucial for downstream robot performance after fine-tuning, while visual track prediction and training with future-force prediction improve dexterous execution. Experiments varying the human-robot data ratio during fine-tuning further suggest that FACT learns from human demonstrations nearly as effectively as from robot demonstrations.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: End-to-End Vision-Language-Action Policies for Autonomous Lunar Rover Docking
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Sitan Huang, Grace Gao
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: This paper presents an end-to-end vision-language-action policy for lunar rover docking, demonstrating competitive performance against modular navigation under perceptual disturbances with adaptive execution for safety.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Surface navigation on the Moon is subject to extreme illumination contrast and deployment-time perceptual disturbances. While modular navigation pipelines have long supported planetary rover navigation, robustness is compromised by measurement errors that propagate through hand-engineered components. End-to-end learned policies are an alternative approach to navigation, which maps observations directly to control actions without intermediate components. Vision-language-action models, in particular, have driven significant breakthroughs in robotics and autonomous vehicle research. By leveraging internet-scale vision-language pretraining, these models can be exploited for their commonsense reasoning and visual understanding to provide robust generalization with limited task-specific data. However, their applicability and performance have yet to be characterized for lunar surface operations. In this study, we design a vision-language-action policy for autonomous lunar rover docking and characterize its performance relative to a modular navigation pipeline. We develop a scalable training framework that generates safety-aware expert demonstrations in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. In closed-loop evaluations, our policy performs competitively relative to the modular baseline under perceptual disturbances unseen during training. To address the tradeoff between compute consumption and closed-loop safety, the policy adapts its execution horizon by determining how far the rover may safely travel in open loop. Adaptive-horizon execution reduces inference frequency while limiting hazard-contact rates relative to fixed horizons in the evaluated scenarios.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Full-Order Safety for Nonlinear Reduced-Order MPC
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Luis Pabon, Johannes Köhler, Revant Kasichainula, Marco Pavone
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: CoRE-MPC ensures safety and efficiency in nonlinear model predictive control by using robust reduced-order models, maintaining constraint satisfaction while significantly reducing computational demands.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Reduced-order models (ROMs) make model predictive control (MPC) of high-dimensional nonlinear systems tractable, but the resulting modeling error can lead to constraint violations on the real system. We introduce CoRE-MPC, a robust MPC formulation that plans with a nonlinear ROM and guarantees recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction for the full-order system. It can be applied with a broad class of nonlinear model reduction techniques and the resulting MPC does not require evaluating the full-order model online, thus ensuring computational efficiency. The key insight is in how the ROM affects the dynamics of the prediction error. We account for this with two error radii that are propagated alongside the ROM and provide a guaranteed bound on the prediction error. The approach is validated in simulation on an 80-state oscillator chain, a Burgers equation, and a 9,768-state finite-element soft robot, where a two-state ROM with data-driven bounds keeps all 1,628 nodes clear of a wall at a median solve time below 1 ms for a 20 ms control period. Across these examples, CoRE-MPC is 13 to 61 times faster than full-order robust MPC at only 27 to 35% higher closed-loop cost, whereas existing certified schemes are either infeasible or at least twice as conservative. Code: [released upon publication].

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Back on Track: Deployment-time Policy Improvement via World Model Planning
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Colton Crosby, Hao Wang, Mac Schwager, Somil Bansal
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The paper presents a framework that enhances visuomotor policy performance during deployment by using a world model for real-time monitoring and corrective planning.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: State-of-the-art visuomotor policies are increasingly capable of executing complex tasks, yet can fail during deployment in ways they cannot predict or recover from on their own. Improving their performance and robustness typically requires collecting more data, retraining, or modifying the policy architecture, all of which are time- and resource-intensive in practice. We instead propose an offline-trained monitoring-and-intervention framework that improves a policy during deployment using only black-box query access. From a limited set of labeled on-policy rollouts, we learn a policy-conditioned liveness value that measures the nominal policy's progress toward task completion; we additionally train a compact latent world model using these rollouts together with play data. At deployment, the liveness value continuously monitors execution. When it detects a loss of progress, a short-horizon planner searches the world model for corrective actions using the same value as its planning objective, after which control returns to the nominal policy. We evaluate our method on the LIBERO-Goal task suite and on a Franka Panda manipulator, using the vision-language-action model $π_{0.5}$ and a diffusion policy as nominal policies, and demonstrate significant improvements in task success rates, while supporting real-time control. Additional results and videos are available on the project website (https://policy-improvement-wm.pages.dev/).

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Efficient Noise Context-Aware Representation for Low-Dose CT Denoising
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Minwoo Yu, N. Robert Bennett, Jongduk Baek, Adam S. Wang
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The ENCORE framework enhances low-dose CT denoising by leveraging specific noise characteristics and anatomical features, improving quality and efficiency through adaptive convolution and zero-shot conditional denoising.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: While deep learning-based denoising has become widely adopted in low-dose CT, conventional models use generic architectures designed for natural images, failing to account for non-stationary and spatially correlated CT noise characteristics. To address this, we propose an Efficient Noise COntext-aware REpresentation (ENCORE) framework that explicitly leverages CT noise characteristics and anatomical features. First, we reformulate the noise synthesis procedure based on a realistic noise distribution beyond the conventional Gaussian approximation, establishing a rigorous foundation for training pair generation. Next, we extract local noise power and correlation contexts to guide the denoising process. To fully leverage the potential of noise context, we propose a FlyingConv module, which adaptively changes convolution weights for each local image region. Notably, our approach demonstrates substantial gains in both denoising quality and computational efficiency. Furthermore, manipulating the intensity of the noise context maps at inference time enables zero-shot conditional denoising, allowing for dynamic control over the output image texture. The entire pipeline is available at https://github.com/minwoo-yu/ENCORE.git

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: FoveaVLA: Foveation Actions Replace the Wrist Camera in VLAs
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Bingao Chen, Lihan Zha, C. Karen Liu, Guy Tevet
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: FoveaVLA enhances Vision-Language-Action models by using learned foveation actions to replace wrist cameras, improving manipulation success rates in complex tasks.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: We present FoveaVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that replaces the wrist camera with learned foveation actions. Wrist cameras provide close-up detail but restrict the view to the end-effector's surroundings. External cameras see the whole scene, but the policy receives them at low resolution, so the fine detail needed for manipulation is lost. FoveaVLA recovers this detail by predicting, alongside each action chunk, the interaction region to observe at the next policy query. The policy then receives crops of these regions, taken from the original-resolution images, together with the full views. We build FoveaVLA on $π_{0.5}$ in two configurations, Single and Dual, using one or two external stereo cameras with full and foveal RGB and depth inputs, and post-train both on DROID with RoboInter interaction annotations. Across four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.8% success with one external RGB-D view, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.1%, versus 52.1% for the wrist-equipped $π_{0.5}$. Both match the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improve success with distractors, cloth manipulation, and far-away objects.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Kaifei Wang, Zikang Shan, Liwei Wang, Yinyu Ye, Han Zhong
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: This paper investigates the role of bias-corrected exponential moving average momentum in reinforcement learning, demonstrating that optimal momentum selection enhances performance in policy gradient optimization.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training. Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, where the EMA coefficient $β$ controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly, we prove that increasing $β$ within a range that prevents overshoot strictly accelerates optimization. When gradients are estimated from sampled responses, a positive expected gain can be obscured by sampling fluctuations. We show that as the learning rate $η$ decreases, the expected gain with fixed $β$ vanishes faster than these fluctuations, whereas increasing $β$ to keep $η/(1-β)$ within the safe regime preserves a nonvanishing gain that eventually dominates them. Bandit simulations quantitatively validate these predictions. RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base using SGD with EMA and AdamW support our principle of choosing larger coefficients in practical LLM post-training. On Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, simply increasing $β_1$ improves mean validation accuracy by nearly $2$ percentage points over the conventional choice, demonstrating the principle's effectiveness at a larger model scale.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: PanTact: Teaching Whole-Body Dexterity with a Wearable Contact Interface
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Xiaomeng Xu, Han Zhang, Zhian Ruan, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: PanTact enables humanoid robots to learn whole-body dexterity through a wearable interface that captures human demonstrations, facilitating manipulation beyond hand-centric approaches.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Humanoid robots have many degrees of freedom and contact surfaces, yet most loco-manipulation research restricts manipulation to the hands and avoids other body contacts with the environment. To extend manipulation beyond the hands, we present PanTact, a system that learns humanoid whole-body dexterity, the capability to manipulate with any suitable body surface, directly from robot-free human demonstrations. Our key idea is to use contact as manipulation-centric information that transfers across embodiments. Contact locations and timing specify the interactions needed to accomplish a task, while the robot chooses how to coordinate its body to realize them within its own physical constraints. Specifically, PanTact captures, learns, and executes whole-body contact via: 1) a wearable, robot-free data collection interface that augments egocentric vision and bimanual UMI grippers with whole-body modular contact patches to record body contact locations and states; 2) a visuomotor policy that mitigates the egocentric observation gap and predicts whole-body contact goals; and 3) contact-aware whole-body control formulations that realize active contact goals using suitable robot surfaces. We deploy PanTact on a Unitree G1 humanoid without additional body contact sensors, demonstrating whole-body dexterity involving body support, pushing, sweeping, and load-sharing. Website: https://pantact.github.io

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: MagicBeanStalk: Escaping the RLVR Zero Advantage Trap with Recursive Data Synthesis
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Ximing Lu, Aviral Kumar, Jan Kautz, Yejin Choi, David Acuna
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: MagicBeanStalk introduces a recursive data-synthesis algorithm that effectively generates calibrated training problems for RLVR, significantly improving model performance across various benchmarks.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Data-centric scaling of RLVR has focused on collecting or generating verifiable training problems. However, corpus size alone does not determine whether the dataset provides a useful learning signal for a target policy. To guide the synthesis of effective RLVR data, we experimentally characterize dataset effectiveness as a function of its problems, the target policy, and the training rollout budget. Under this characterization, we show that a large open-source math corpus pooled from widely used RLVR datasets falls almost entirely into a zero-advantage trap: for a fixed target policy and rollout budget, roughly 88% of its problems are solved in every rollout or failed in every rollout. Filtering concentrates what remains, but it can only select, discarding the hard problems. Effective synthetic problems should therefore require the reasoning operations and compositions required to solve those hard problems. Yet their difficulty must be calibrated, so that some rollouts succeed, some fail, and at least one correct solution fits within the training budget. Prompting a teacher to vary hard problems directly does not achieve this. Guided by these empirical principles, we introduce MagicBeanStalk, a top-down decomposition and bottom-up recursive data-synthesis algorithm that grows seed problems into families of substantively new, policy- and budget-calibrated training problems while preserving the seeds' reasoning blueprints. Across 8 math benchmarks, continual RLVR on MagicBeanStalk problems improves gpt-oss-120b from 61.2 to 69.8 (+8.6) and DeepSeek v4Flash from 72.4 to 77.9 (+5.4) on a 16K-token budget. Training on the full 78K source corpus improves by only +1.1 and its best filtered real data subset by +5.8. In finance, we synthesize over 14K verifiable problems from only 340 solutions and improve over base by 6.9 and 2.4 points on SecQue and FinanceBench, respectively.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: FallGown: A Soft Pneumatic Wearable Device for Fall Prevention
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Megan C. Coram, Haoran Lei, Steven H. Collins, Steve B. Cousins, Michelle Baldonado
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The FallGown is a lightweight, soft pneumatic wearable device designed to prevent falls in older adults, offering support while enabling mobility and monitored exercise.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Concerns about falling and potential resulting injuries prevent many older adults from participating in forms of health-improving exercise such as walking, dance, and tai chi. Existing passive devices like walkers require use of the arms for support, and active devices like exoskeletons and robotic frames are often rigid, bulky, and stigmatized, which limits their use. The FallGown is a soft wearable support structure consisting of pressurized pneumatic pouches within a fabric shell; it can support the full weight of a user's body and aims to prevent falls. It is portable (6.9 kg and 0.051 m3 when stored), minimally burdensome (7.24-20.8 N drag force depending on floor type and whether an optional rolling base frame is used), and convenient (less than 2.5 minutes on average to don and less than 0.5 minutes on average to doff). The optional rolling base lowers friction with the floor, but reduces portability and skirt deformation (which can be useful to fit through doors and other tight spaces). Fall prevention testing with a single user revealed a tradeoff between device size and stability against tipping; a skirt with 12 pneumatic pouches and a floor diameter of 1.4 meters with a base frame prevented all falls except in one case with a mechanical failure. On-board pressure sensors can sense the user's weight distribution, providing an opportunity for monitored exercise and adaptive support.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Reflex: Visually Grounded Reactive Humanoid Control
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Taoyang Jia, Weikai Huang, Linxin Song, Jared Darlington, Jieyu Zhao
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: Reflex is a novel framework enabling humanoid robots to catch thrown boxes by integrating whole-body control, real-time object dynamics inference, and egocentric visual perception.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Humans effortlessly react to the world; they adeptly return a tennis shot, catch a falling cup, step aside from a passing cart, or pass a box tossed during truck unloading. These everyday actions require anticipating a moving target and reflexively responding with the whole body within about a second. Such visual reactive whole-body control remains challenging for humanoids, which must (1) coordinate whole-body control, (2) react to object dynamics in real time, and (3) ground perception in egocentric vision. We study catching thrown boxes as a representative task that demands all three capabilities; existing systems cover only part of it, relying on end-effectors, motion capture, or marked objects. We present Reflex, a three-stage framework that learns these capabilities stage by stage while connecting them through a compact representation of object dynamics. First, a state-based policy learns whole-body catching with reinforcement learning. Second, the policy learns to infer the dynamics of a moving box from delayed and incomplete observations. Third, an egocentric RGB-D encoder learns to recover this dynamics representation directly from visual observations while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. This decomposition provides each capability with a direct training signal and makes visual learning substantially more scalable. In simulation, Reflex achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% when given privileged box observations. Temporal visual history is critical: removing it reduces success by 35.6 and 39.8 points on centered and laterally offset throws. On a real Unitree G1, Reflex catches human-thrown boxes with 65% and 40% success at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of human catchers' success at the same distances.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: BT-Agent: Deploying Onboard Robot Agents with Behavior Trees and Multi-Fidelity Evaluation
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Fabio Hübel, Adam Lilja, Yue Yin, Siming He, Claire Tomlin
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: BT-Agent integrates LLM-driven task reasoning with behavior-tree skills for efficient onboard robot operation, demonstrating improved performance and evaluation through a novel multi-fidelity benchmark.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Deploying language-model agents onboard mobile robots requires task reasoning and responsive execution within limited compute and memory. We propose BT-Agent, an onboard architecture combining LLM-driven task decisions with predefined behavior-tree (BT) skills. These skills enforce execution conditions and return structured failure feedback. We demonstrate fully onboard operation with a 9B model on a quadruped across five task categories. Intervention tests show that local checks stop ongoing navigation without waiting for another model decision, while the agent remains active to retry or report constraints. To compare agent designs efficiently, we introduce a 161-task multi-fidelity benchmark, evaluated in text on all tasks and in Habitat on 39. Text supports 10.9$\times$ higher evaluation throughput, while simulation reveals how perception and motion failures change task outcomes. BT-Agent's largest success gains over the strongest Act/ReAct baseline occur at 4B and 9B: approximately 10 and 5 percentage points. Ablations identify structured tool calls and informative failure feedback as the most useful components.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Chronos Policy: Learning Robot Policies on Physical Time
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Changhao Wang, Jaden Clark, Shuran Song
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: Chronos Policy enhances robot learning by explicitly incorporating physical time into action sequences, improving performance on dynamic and multisensory tasks while maintaining robustness in quasi-static scenarios.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Robot policies often convert sensing and control into fixed-rate observation-action sequences, leaving physical time implicit in sequence position. This assumption breaks when observation rates or delays vary, or when inference latency changes. We introduce Chronos Policy, which makes physical time explicit by conditioning on observation capture times and desired action execution times. We study two ways to incorporate time into a diffusion transformer: adding timestamp embeddings to token features, or encoding physical time in positional encoding through time-aware rotary positional encodings (time-aware RoPE). We find that time-aware RoPE is more robust, allowing attention to depend directly on physical time while keeping token content unchanged. During training, we temporally randomize which observations are sampled and when the action chunk begins, exposing the policy to a wider range of sensing and execution schedules that may occur during deployments. This also enables learning from asynchronous, multi-rate data without forcing all measurements onto a fixed temporal grid. Across simulation and real-world experiments, Chronos Policy improves performance on dynamic tasks, where observation-to-action timing is critical, and on multisensory tasks, where the relative timing between observations matters. On standard quasi-static tasks, it preserves nominal performance while improving robustness to changes in sensing and inference timing.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Manthan Patel, Jonas Frey, Mayank Mittal, Fan Yang, Alexander Hansson
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: DeFM is a self-supervised foundation model for depth images that enhances robotic task performance and generalization through geometric and semantic representation learning.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Depth sensors are widely deployed across robotic platforms, and advances in fast, high-fidelity depth simulation have enabled robotic policies trained on depth observations to achieve robust sim-to-real transfer for a wide range of tasks. Despite this, representation learning for depth modality remains underexplored compared to RGB, where large-scale foundation models now define the state of the art. To address this gap, we present DeFM, a self-supervised foundation model trained entirely on depth images for robotic applications. Using a DINO-style self-distillation objective on a curated dataset of 60M depth images, DeFM learns geometric and semantic representations that generalize to diverse environments, tasks, and sensors. To retain metric awareness across multiple scales, we introduce a novel input normalization strategy. We further distill DeFM into compact models suitable for resource-constrained robotic systems. When evaluated on depth-based classification, segmentation, navigation, locomotion, and manipulation benchmarks, DeFM achieves state-of-the-art performance and demonstrates strong generalization from simulation to real-world environments. We release all our pretrained models, which can be adopted off-the-shelf for depth-based robotic learning without task-specific fine-tuning. Webpage: https://de-fm.github.io/

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Injecting Hallucinations in Autonomous Vehicles: A Component-Agnostic Safety Evaluation Framework
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Alexandre Moreira Nascimento, Gabriel Kenji Godoy Shimanuki, Lúcio Flavio Vismari, João Batista Camargo, Jorge Rady de Almeida
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: This paper presents a configurable framework for injecting perception hallucinations in autonomous vehicles, enhancing safety evaluation by quantifying their impact on collision risks in simulations.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Perception failures in autonomous vehicles (AV) remain a major safety concern because they can directly compromise decision-making and contribute to unsafe behavior. To study how these failures affect safety, researchers typically inject artificial faults into real-world or simulated components and observe the resulting outcomes. However, existing fault injection (FI) studies often target a single sensor within the machine perception (MP) module, resulting in siloed frameworks that are difficult to generalize or integrate into unified simulation environments. This work addresses that limitation by reframing perception failures as hallucinations, that is, false perceptions that distort an AV's situational awareness and may trigger unsafe control actions. Building on this concept, we propose a configurable, component-agnostic hallucination injection framework that induces six plausible hallucination types in an open-source simulation environment. A total of 18,356 simulations (8,695 baseline and 9,661 with hallucinations injected) were executed while AVs crossed an unsignalized intersection with transversal traffic. The results statistically validate the framework and quantify the impact of each hallucination type on collisions and on the minimum distance between the AV and the nearest vehicle, used as a continuous proxy for the safety margin. Certain hallucinations, especially missed detection, blind region, angular drift, phantom perception, and latency, significantly increase the odds of collision, while linear drift significantly reduces minimum distances without producing a statistically significant increase in collision odds in the evaluated scenario. The proposed framework provides a scalable and statistically grounded method for evaluating AV safety under perception distortions and supports future research on fault tolerance and resilient AV design.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Infinite-Dimensional Closed-Loop Inverse Kinematics for Soft Robots via Neural Operators
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Carina Veil, Moritz Flaschel, Ellen Kuhl, Cosimo Della Santina
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: This paper presents an infinite-dimensional closed-loop inverse kinematics approach for soft robots, utilizing neural operators to learn actuation-to-shape mappings and derive task-specific control.
