A flow-share readout of the trained flow, invariant to the backward policy, and a separate signed utility rank which skills to change, verifier evidence decides whether an edit is warranted, and a residual-variance plateau sets when to update. Committed edits reshape the graph the next policy learns on, realizing recursive skill evolution. Across question answering, mathematical reasoning, interactive decision making, and code generation, R$^2$ Flow improves task accuracy and library-edit precision over heuristic orchestration, reinforcement learning, and skill-evolution baselines, and transfers across executors. Code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/r2flow.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: TriFold: Folding irregular 3D Gaussians into structured latents for 3D Scene Generation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yun Wang, Chiyu Wang, Fan Jiang, Ziyu Zhu, Zhaoxu Sun
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: TriFold introduces a 3D Gaussian VAE that encodes complex scenes into structured latents, enhancing reconstruction and generation through adaptive spatial representation and occupancy prediction.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Recent progress in 3D generation has motivated growing interest in compact generative representations of complex 3D scenes. For native 3D Gaussian scenes, however, learning such representations remains challenging due to widely varying primitive counts, nonuniform spatial density, and differences in geometry and appearance even among spatially neighboring primitives. In this work, we introduce TriFold, a native 3D Gaussian VAE that encodes Gaussian scenes into a fixed-layout triplane latent and jointly reconstructs their geometry and appearance. The key insight is to impose structural regularity on the latent space while preserving the spatial adaptivity of the underlying Gaussians. During encoding, we use cell-wise learned queries to aggregate projected Gaussians into multiple slots per cell, reducing the information loss caused by single-feature pooling. During decoding, occupancy prediction identifies active regions, where query-based set prediction and candidate selection reconstruct local Gaussian sets with spatially varying primitive counts. Building on this representation, we train a latent flow-matching model for conditional scene-level 3DGS generation, enabling point-cloud-conditioned synthesis and single-image-conditioned amodal generation. Experiments demonstrate that TriFold achieves high-fidelity reconstruction and generation from a single image that provides only a partial observation of the scene, validating its effectiveness for native 3D Gaussian representation learning. https://fantasy-amap.github.io/TriFold

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: NativeMEM: Native Memory Compression for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Ziye Wang, Modi Shi, Chaojun Ni, Jiazhi Yang, Mengdi Li
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: NativeMEM introduces an efficient memory compression method for Vision-Language-Action models, enhancing long-horizon robotic manipulation performance while reducing latency and memory usage.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: How can pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models retain long-horizon visual histories with high-frequency updates without sacrificing efficiency? Existing approaches rely on external memory management, which restrains either the memory horizon or the reactiveness of pretrained policies. To this end, we present NativeMEM, a VLA policy that features long-term and real-time updated memory. At its core is an efficient memory encoding scheme, Native Memory Compression, which repurposes the VLA's own vision encoder to compress each historical frame from each camera view into a single token. Appended to the input sequence, these memory tokens enable the pretrained VLA to attend over long-term history with negligible latency overhead, requiring neither an external planner nor a freshly initialized memory module. To align the memory tokens with the pretrained policy, we first develop a generic memory tokenizer under the supervision of a frozen VLA on memory-demanding data, and then unfreeze the VLA for task-specific fine-tuning. NativeMEM consistently outperforms prior methods, boosting success rates from 32.4% to 84.0% in simulation and up to 98.7% on real robots, while maintaining low inference latency and GPU memory usage. Notably, NativeMEM exhibits high data efficiency by achieving competitive results with prior arts using only 20% of the training data.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Execution Before Memory: Diagnosing Memory Failures in Video World Models
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Weiyang Jin, Jiwen Yu, Sihan Xu, Yuwei Niu, Xihui Liu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper introduces MIST for diagnosing memory failures in video world models, proposing M3-Agent to enhance execution accuracy and significantly improve evaluation scores.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: A memory test for a video world model should say whether the scene was set, whether the asked change was carried out, and whether the last frame shows the result. Current tests fold these into one number, so a low score is easy to read as forgetting. When the change is not carried out, the hidden state transition cannot appear, so the test is not really a test of memory. We introduce MIST, an evaluation that separates the change from the memory it should leave behind. The model first sets the scene while the change stays hidden, and only later is asked to show it, with leakage before that point kept under control. This separation locates the bottleneck: the model sets the scene but does not carry out the instructed change. The same gap appears in general memory evaluations. On that basis we propose M3-Agent (Make the Missing Move), which recursively revises the details of the input instruction so that the model successfully carries out the requested instruction. Relative to the baseline, it more than triples the MIST reveal score. On the benchmarks, WRBench's score T rises by 26.1% and MBench-T's score U by 52.7%. The method meets the problem from the execution side: it shows what the frozen model can do once the move is stated, and it sets a stricter baseline.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: From Trajectories to Differentiated Skills: Cognitive Differentiation for Self-Improving Agents
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yewei Zhao, Derong Xu, Wei Chen, Yin Xu, Peilun Zhou
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper introduces Cognitive Differentiation in Skill Evolution (CDSE), enhancing agent performance by evolving skills through coordinated, functionally distinct components, achieving superior results across multiple benchmarks.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents tackle complex tasks through reasoning and interaction with external environments. Agent skills provide persistent, transferable capabilities that guide task planning, inform contextual decisions, support tool use, and enable executable procedures. Yet existing skill-evolution methods largely organize knowledge around skill artifacts, overlooking the functional heterogeneity within individual skills and its implications for knowledge maintenance and use. Inspired by cognitive science, we propose Cognitive Differentiation in Skill Evolution (CDSE), which evolves a unified skill through four functionally distinct yet coordinated components: Meta, Experience, Tool, and Script. CDSE extracts evidence-grounded semantic gradients from successful and failed trajectories, consolidates them by functional role, and applies component-specific updates and validation with cross-component coordination and adaptive invocation. An analysis of 500 top-ranked skill packages shows that 96.8% contain knowledge spanning at least two functional roles. Across six benchmarks, three agent models, and two execution harnesses, CDSE achieves the highest scores in all 36 settings, improving over the Base agent by 7.6 percentage points and the strongest competing method in each setting by 2.6 points on average. Ablation studies further support the importance of functional differentiation and adaptive invocation.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: FlexPart: Text-Controlled Semantics-Aware 3D Part Segmentation at Flexible Granularity
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yiqun Zhao, Jiachen Xu, Yihao Zhi, Yunfei Zhao, Zibo Zhao
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: FLEXPART is a novel framework for text-controlled 3D mesh segmentation that enables flexible, semantics-aware part extraction, outperforming existing models in accuracy and granularity.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: A 3D asset admits multiple valid part decompositions, while semantics-aware segmentation should reflect both the desired granularity and the parts a user wants to extract. Ideally, a practical segmentation model should strive for a simple principle: what you ask for is what you get. However, realizing this goal is hindered by two core obstacles: the lack of multi-granularity training data and the absence of a holistic control mechanism. We propose FLEXPART, a unified framework for text-controlled 3D mesh segmentation. To establish flexible control, we introduce a holistic control prompt comprising semantic part names with location and shape clauses. To support this mechanism, we utilize an automated Vision-Language Model (VLM) pipeline to construct a large-scale dataset of multi-granularity partitions and their corresponding prompts. Driven by this data, FLEXPART generates a view-independent part-identity field in native 3D space, directly assigning discrete part IDs to mesh faces. To compel the model to respect semantic conditions rather than rely on geometric priors, we train the model using randomized background dropping. Furthermore, an inference-time VLM planner can automatically complete descriptive clauses from 2D renderings, allowing users to simply name the desired parts in ordinary words. FLEXPART with planner-completed prompts outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline by 15% in mIoU, even when that baseline receives ground-truth guidance. On our held-out FLEXPARTBENCH, FLEXPART leads at each granularity and improves average mIoU by 22% over the strongest baseline. With only the requested part names supplied by the user, it also improves IoU by 35% over the strongest click-driven baseline on selective segmentation.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: R$^2$Orch: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Orchestration via Self-Play within a Skill-Internalization Loop
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Mingda Zhang, Yun Huang, Qiang Huang, Yanjin Li, Rui Qian
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: R$^2$Orch introduces a recursive self-play framework for agent orchestration that enhances skill learning and evaluation, outperforming traditional methods across various complex tasks.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: In recent years, agentic orchestration has been widely applied to solve complex human tasks. However, existing orchestration learning still faces key challenges, including hand-designed curricula, advantage collapse when a task's rollouts all reach the same outcome, and unreliable evaluation signals that judge each skill by one noisy score. To address these challenges, we propose R$^2$Orch, a new paradigm of Recursive Self-Play Orchestration: an inner loop of self-play that improves the orchestrator on self-chosen tasks, and an outer loop that improves how the inner loop improves. To support this paradigm, we introduce Recursive Learnability, a training objective that rewards a Proposer for choosing tasks whose rollouts keep reaching different outcomes as skills are withdrawn. Built on this objective, we further propose Skill Withdrawal, in which the outer loop withdraws each skill once a controlled evaluation within self-play shows that the orchestrator performs as well without it. Moreover, the two loops form one cycle: failures are distilled into skills, skills into parameters, and withdrawals lead the Proposer to new failures, so the orchestrator moves toward zero-skill deployment. Experimental results on twelve datasets show that R$^2$Orch consistently outperforms baselines across question answering, math, code, and interactive tasks.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Reward Engine: Reward-Centric Self-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Litong Feng, Ji Qi, Yiran Cheng, Shaowu Pan, Xinyu Zhang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The Reward Engine constructs a stable, experience-based reward system for open-ended tool agents, improving execution consistency and aligning closely with benchmark evaluations.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Open-ended tool agents can complete the same objective through different tool paths, and their quality depends jointly on the interaction trace, environment state, and final artifacts, so such tasks rarely admit an executable ground-truth reward. The central challenge is therefore to construct a reward from existing experience that exposes the current policy's failures while remaining stationary during optimization. We introduce Reward Engine, which, like a self-motivated student, first works out what success requires and then optimizes toward it. From the task and initial trajectories, it builds a RewardPack of testcases for required correctness and rubrics for graded quality, each executed as a check that returns a judgment with evidence. The frozen RewardPack then guides the agent to revise and select its outputs, and can also serve as a reward for reinforcement learning. On WorkBuddy Bench Office and Claw-Eval, the constructed reward largely agrees with the benchmark graders, not reversing their ordering on 82.3\% and 80.5\% of candidate pairs. Used to revise executions, it raises three-run consistency ($\mathrm{Pass}^{3}$) over Baseline from 45.0\% to 54.0\% and from 78.4\% to 83.7\%.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Referring Multi-Object Tracking with Diverse Dynamic Expressions
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yani Zhang, Dongming Wu, Wencheng Han, Xingping Dong, Shengcai Liao
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: This paper introduces referring multi-object tracking (RMOT) to enhance object localization using diverse language expressions and a novel Transformer-based framework, TempRMOT, achieving state-of-the-art results.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Referring understanding is a fundamental task that bridges natural language and visual content by localizing objects described in free-form expressions. However, existing works are constrained by limited language expressiveness, lacking the capacity to model object dynamics in spatial numbers and temporal states. To address these limitations, we introduce a new and general referring understanding task, termed referring multi-object tracking (RMOT). Its core idea is to employ a language expression as a semantic cue to guide the prediction of multi-object tracking, comprehensively accounting for variations in object quantity and temporal semantics. Along with RMOT, we introduce a RMOT benchmark named Refer-KITTI-V2, featuring scalable and diverse language expressions. To efficiently generate high-quality annotations covering object dynamics with minimal manual effort, we propose a semi-automatic labeling pipeline that formulates a total of 9,758 language prompts. In addition, we propose TempRMOT, an elegant end-to-end Transformer-based framework for RMOT. At its core is a query-driven Temporal Enhancement Module that represents each object as a Transformer query, enabling long-term spatial-temporal interactions with other objects and past frames to efficiently refine these queries. TempRMOT achieves state-of-the-art performance on both Refer-KITTI and Refer-KITTI-V2, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. The source code and dataset is available at https://github.com/zyn213/TempRMOT.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Agentic Physics-Grounded Video Generation via Memory-Augmented In-Context Reasoning
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Xikang Guan, Shaocong Yang, Yanqi Bao, Can Wang, Zheng Gu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: PhysRepair enhances video generation by diagnosing and selectively repairing physical inconsistencies using causal reasoning and prior repair experiences, improving realism across various physics domains.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Physical plausibility is essential for realistic video generation. Existing methods impose physical guidance before synthesis via simulations or refined prompts, but this can limit dynamic diversity, miss errors that emerge only after generation, and require repeated regeneration when inconsistencies remain. We therefore study a generate-diagnose-repair paradigm that preserves the original generation capability and selectively repairs physical inconsistencies afterward, raising two key questions: what to repair and how to repair? To address them, we introduce PhysRepair, an agentic video generation framework that combines causal reasoning over the observed physical failure with prior repair experience to enable localized and adaptive correction. Specifically, Spatiotemporal Causal Constraints identify the first invalid physical state and its causally affected states, producing a repair specification that guides physically plausible local regeneration while preserving unaffected content. Experience-augmented In-context Learning combines the ongoing repair context with relevant experience from previous repairs, allowing the agent to adapt its repair decisions across diverse physical failures and accumulate completed trajectories for future cases. Experiments on Physics-IQ Verified across solid mechanics, fluid dynamics, optics, thermodynamics, and magnetism demonstrate that PhysRepair consistently improves the physical plausibility of generated videos over existing methods. Our project page is available at https://xxkkxxx.github.io/PhysRepair-Website/.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Imagine Before You Predict: Interleaved Latent Visual Reasoning for Video Event Prediction
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Tianxiang Jiang, Linquan Wu, Sheng Xia, Songze Li, Ziang Yan
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: Future-L1 introduces an interleaved latent visual reasoning framework for video event prediction, enhancing accuracy by preserving visual semantics during autoregressive decoding, achieving state-of-the-art results.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Video event prediction (VEP) requires models to infer unobserved future states from partial video evidence. Existing video MLLMs usually verbalize intermediate future reasoning in text space: once visual evidence is verbalized, fine-grained motion, geometry, and interaction cues can be lost, leading to plausible but visually ungrounded hallucinations. We introduce Future-L1, an interleaved latent visual reasoning framework that lets an MLLM alternate between language tokens and continuous latent visual spans during autoregressive decoding. To train this capability, we construct Future-L1-50K by selecting examples where future visual hints help prediction and align latent states to future-frame embeddings, then further optimize sampled latent trajectories with LA-DAPO, a latent-aware RL objective with outcome-contrastive and temporal-diversity rewards. Future-L1 achieves new state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks: on FutureBench, it improves Qwen3-VL-8B from 61.0 to 85.4 and exceeds the previous best Video-CoE by 10.4 points; on TwiFF-Bench, it improves the average score from 2.44 to 3.04. These results suggest that future-oriented video reasoning benefits from preserving intermediate visual semantics in latent space rather than translating every reasoning step into text.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: PhyMix: Towards Physically Consistent Single-Image 3D Indoor Scene Generation with Implicit--Explicit Optimization
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Dongli Wu, Jingyu Hu, Ka-Hei Hui, Xiaobao Wei, Chengwen Luo
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: PhyMix introduces a framework that integrates a Physics Evaluator to enhance physical consistency in single-image 3D indoor scene generation, improving reliability for robotics and AI applications.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Existing methods for single-image 3D indoor scene generation often produce visually plausible results that violate real-world physical constraints, limiting their reliability in robotics, embodied AI, and virtual environment design. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Physics Evaluator that assesses four aspects (geometric priors, contact, stability, and deployability) through nine sub-constraints, establishing a benchmark for evaluating physical consistency. Our analysis reveals that even state-of-the-art methods produce scenes with substantial physical inconsistencies despite their visual plausibility. To address these limitations, we propose a framework that incorporates feedback from the Physics Evaluator into both training and inference to improve the physical plausibility of generated scenes. Specifically, PhyMix comprises two components: (i) implicit alignment via Scene-GRPO, a critic-free group-relative preference optimization strategy that uses physical evaluations to guide the generator toward physically plausible layouts, and (ii) explicit refinement via verifier-guided agentic repair, which translates evaluator diagnostics into executable scene-editing skills to correct residual violations at inference time. PhyMix unifies physical evaluation, preference-based alignment, and agentic inference-time correction to improve physical plausibility while retaining the observed scene content. Experiments show improvements in reconstruction quality and physical plausibility, while qualitative examples on stylized and real-world images illustrate the applicability of the framework beyond synthetic inputs.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: ReTerm: Recovery Training for Self-Improving Terminal Agents
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Wei Xie, Kaituo Feng, Shiming Fu, Yong Liu, Xiangyu Yue
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: ReTerm enhances terminal agents' error recovery through self-improvement training, utilizing a custom dataset and an online RL algorithm, significantly boosting task completion rates.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Terminal agents have shown strong abilities in complex coding tasks. However, they often struggle to recover from errors during long-running execution (e.g., command errors, faulty implementations), eventually leading to task failures. To this end, we present ReTerm, a self-improving terminal agent trained by learning how to recover from its own failed terminal tasks. To support its training, we construct a customized data pipeline and produce ReTerm-10K, a high-quality dataset that provides effective recovery demonstrations for SFT cold start. Furthermore, we propose ReTerm-GRPO, an online RL algorithm that forks from the agent's own failure states to generate multiple independent self-recovery attempts. By learning from whether these attempts successfully complete the task, the agent self-improves through its own recovery experience. Built on Qwen3.5-9B, our ReTerm-9B achieves 34.8% Pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2.0, improving over the base model by 14.6 points. Further analysis shows that our method achieves consistently higher recovery rates across diverse error categories compared with standard GRPO training. All code, data and model are released at https://github.com/twothsnd/ReTerm.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: RoPE-Flow: Monocular Vision-based Robot Pose Estimation via 2D Graph-Conditioned 3D Flow Matching
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Liangjing Shao, Wanhao Liu, Zhiwei Fang, Rulin Zhou, Quanlu Zhang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: RoPE-Flow introduces an end-to-end framework for monocular robot pose estimation using flow matching, enhancing accuracy and consistency through innovative feature extraction and loss functions.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Camera-to-robot pose estimation from a monocular image is significant for vision-based robot navigation and control. However, recovering 3D structural features from 2D observations remains a challenging task. Existing camera-to-robot pose estimation methods either rely on time-consuming iterative rendering or involve sophisticated 2D-3D registration which suffers from projection ambiguity, accumulated errors for distal joints and imbalanced learning for different joints. In this work, we propose RoPE-Flow, an end-to-end flow matching-based framework for camera-to-robot pose estimation. From the predicted 2D heatmaps, we propose a Keypoint-centered Feature Extractor to obtain positional features along with contextual representations from keypoints-centered multi-scale patches. Moreover, we introduce Graph-guided Condition Generator, which embeds a learnable adjacency map to generate condition for flow matching based on correlation among keypoints. Besides, we introduce Bone Length Loss and Ray-Depth Loss for topological consistency and scale stability, with joint-wise weighting to mitigate varied prediction difficulty across joints. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods for pose estimation across different types of robots with mutiple cameras. Besides, we establish a novel cross-scene benchmark to demonstrate the outstanding performance of RoPE-Flow on zero-shot cross-scene robot pose estimation. Meanwhile, animated visualizations are shown on the website: ropeflow.netlify.app

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: AVALON: Zero-Shot Indoor Navigation with Human-Seeded Topological Memory
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Jing Xia, Changyan Li, Yuduo Wang, Guiyin Tian, Bo Wang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: AVALON enables zero-shot indoor navigation for robots using human-seeded topological memory and evidence-gated co-updating, outperforming existing methods without prior mapping.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Indoor service robots often enter unmapped buildings whose layouts and task constraints are already familiar to users. We address this human-familiar, robot-unseen setting with AVALON, a topological navigation framework organized around human-seeded layered spatial memory, node-verified topological execution, and task-triggered, evidence-gated human--robot memory co-updating. The robot has no prior on-site traversal or site-specific training. Deployment requires only a floor plan, place clues, and an initial topology-odometry alignment. Visual depth point-goal navigation leverages verified node arrivals to perform translational re-anchoring, without requiring a robot-constructed global SLAM map. Human--robot memory co-updating fuses complementary sources of information. Human operators specify task constraints that are unobservable via vision and report offline environmental modifications, whereas the robot provides physical-state evidence through active in-situ validation. Task relevance governs whether human-reported environmental changes undergo robot validation during the active mission. Field-collected perceptual evidence gates memory updates, maintaining an explicit separation between human-specified permissions and robot-observed traversability. Our experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that AVALON with X-NavDP completes a 12.81 m Intersection-to-Dining mission in 46.4 s (5/5) with no mapping, 40.9% less robot time than DimOS-Go2 (78.5 s, 4/5), while policy-only X-NavDP times out in all of the 5 runs. These demonstrate the superiority of the proposed topological navigation framework.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: SPEAR: Selective Preference Elicitation with Adaptive Rewards for VLM-Guided Robotic Manipulation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Zewen Wu, Ruizhe Liu, Pei Zhou, Feng Chen, Yanchao Yang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: SPEAR enhances Vision-Language Models for robotic manipulation by improving query efficiency and exploration, achieving high success rates while reducing abstention and training time.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable automated preference labeling for robotic manipulation, yet their deployment remains impractical since each query incurs substantial inference cost, while VLMs frequently abstain on visually challenging comparisons. We propose SPEAR, a framework that transforms VLMs into efficient preference oracles via two synergistic mechanisms. First, we design distinguishability-aware query selection to reduce abstention rates by targeting only informative and distinguishable comparisons. Second, we deploy an adaptive reward transition that bootstraps exploration with VLM-synthesized guidance before preference-based refinement. Experiments on the manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that SPEAR achieves 88.9% average success, outperforming baselines by 23.3 percentage points, while significantly reducing abstention and wall-clock training time on contact-rich tasks. SPEAR learns three Mobile ALOHA manipulation tasks fully online on real hardware, demonstrating end-to-end real-world applicability. By addressing query efficiency and exploration challenges, SPEAR establishes VLMs as practical preference oracles for scalable robot learning without manual reward engineering.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Seeing Both the Forest and the Trees: Reusing Holistic 3D Priors for Part-Decomposed Generation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yiqun Zhao, Binbin Huang, Haobin Duan, Zibo Zhao, Shenghua Gao
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: STRUCTPARTS introduces a dual-frame coordinate mechanism for part-decomposed 3D generation, leveraging holistic priors to enhance geometric detail and structural coherence efficiently.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Generating 3D assets with explicit parts requires two properties at once: geometric detail inside each part and structural coherence across the whole object. Recent image-conditioned 3D generation models adopt a structured 3D representation that anchors tokens to explicit spatial positions, capturing both properties, but their output remains a single fused mesh. We ask how a part-decomposed generation model can inherit both properties of these holistic priors, and answer with STRUCTPARTS, a framework whose core technical contribution is a dual-frame coordinate interleaving mechanism: each shape latent is interpreted under both a part-local and an object-global reference frame, and processed through a global-local inter-leaved transformer that simultaneously reuses the prior's geometric detail at the part scale and its structural coherence at the whole-object scale. As its structural input, STRUCTPARTS uses a segmented mesh scaffold, a coarse mesh paired with a face-level segmentation mask kept entirely within the prior's native 3D representation. With only lightweight finetuning, both intra-part detail and inter-part coherence emerge from the same pretrained weights. On PartObjaverse-Tiny, STRUCTPARTS matches or surpasses prior part-decomposed models at a fraction of their training cost, while naturally supporting part-mesh refinement and part-level editing.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Anvil: Scaling Embodied Spatial Intelligence through Knowledge Recirculation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Weilin Ruan, Bohan Zhou, Jinghao Li, Yangkai Wei, Wenqian Li
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: Anvil is a unified framework enhancing embodied spatial intelligence through innovative data generation, training, and benchmarking, significantly outperforming existing models in various benchmarks.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Embodied spatial intelligence requires more than visual recognition: models must localize entities, reason about their relations, and express this knowledge in action-relevant forms. Yet joint training can conflate the knowledge needed at different stages because supervision is fragmented across incompatible geometric and semantic outputs. We introduce Anvil, a unified framework for data generation, training, and benchmarking for embodied spatial intelligence. (1) Anvil-Gen is a heterogeneous data flywheel that combines form-specific generation, cross-stage consistency verification, and failure-driven recollection across 11 Ground--Relation--Act forms. (2) Anvil-Ben provides scene-aligned supervision for learning diverse embodied spatial capabilities and scene-linked assessments that distinguish stage competence from error propagation. (3) Anvil-MOPD is a 9B student that consolidates heterogeneous spatial knowledge through distillation from specialist teachers. Semantic-first-fault routing targets teacher supervision to the student's earliest decisive failure, while stage normalization controls the loss scale across native outputs of different lengths. We construct 5.8M source-grounded records spanning 160K images, reserving 580K spatial records for held-out evaluation and using the remaining 5.22M records for training. On average across seven public benchmarks, Anvil-MOPD outperforms Qwen3.5-9B and RynnBrain-8B by 9.29 and 11.03 percentage points, respectively, while reaching 80.67% on VABench-Point. Controlled studies support targeted coverage, selective transfer, and feedback-guided repair as complementary framework components.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: VeriVLA: Adaptive Test-Time Verification for Flow-Based VLAs with Latent World Models
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Xueli Sun, Yuxiang Lu, Yantong Liu, Xianzhe Fan, Xi Chen
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: VeriVLA enhances flow-based VLA policies by adaptively verifying action quality at test time, improving task completion rates across various real-world and simulated scenarios.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are inherently stochastic: different noise seeds can produce action chunks of varying quality from the same observation. At test time, however, the policy typically commits to a single sample without an explicit estimate of its quality. In fine-grained manipulation, executing a suboptimal action can irreversibly disrupt task progress and lead to failure. To exploit policy stochasticity, we introduce a training-free two-axis trigger that uses two initial samples to measure within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance, detecting the critical states. Once triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicting action-conditioned future latent states and the corresponding changes in task progress. By operating in latent space, the verifier avoids pixel reconstruction and enables efficient and more accurate ranking. Across three real-world tasks, $\textit{i.e.,}$ pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement), our method raises the average completion score from 50.8% to 65.5%, while adding 326 ms for sampling and verification per triggered decision on a single RTX 4090. Consistent gains are also observed in simulation, where the average success rate rises from 66.4% to 73.6% in the clean setting of RoboTwin 2.0, from 62.8% to 69.6% in its randomized setting, and from 96.9% to 97.6% on LIBERO.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yilong Xu, Minrui Xu, Xinyu Zhou, Xiang Long, Haochen Tan
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: Mosaic introduces a multi-session agentic reinforcement learning framework that enhances trajectory advantage estimation and session allocation, outperforming traditional methods in efficiency and utility.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Most existing agentic reinforcement learning methods assume single-session trajectories, where interaction proceeds within one continuously accumulated context. However, agentic techniques such as context compaction and subagent forking may produce trajectories spanning multiple sessions, creating a mismatch between the single-session training assumption and inference-time execution. Therefore, we introduce Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, a more general setting that supports an arbitrary number of sessions within a trajectory. Under this setting, a widely adopted method is to broadcast trajectory-level advantages to all sessions, but this does not distinguish contributions from various sessions or guide session allocation within trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Mosaic, a multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization. At the trajectory level, it incorporates session-usage signals into advantage estimation. At the session level, it shapes each session's advantage according to the estimated marginal contribution. Experiments on BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B show that Mosaic outperforms broadcasting in both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average. Further analyses show that our method achieves improvements in session utility and allocation, which we suggested is a promising target for future advances in multi-session agentic RL.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: OS-Helix: Unifying GUI Interaction and Code Execution in Native Computer-Using Agents
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Bowen Yang, Kaiming Jin, Zichen Ding, Zhenyu Wu, Zehao Li
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: OS-Helix is a multimodal agent that integrates GUI interaction and code execution through hybrid training, achieving significant performance improvements in desktop automation tasks.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Real desktop automation is neither purely visual nor purely programmatic. Agents must understand user-facing interfaces while efficiently manipulating files, scripts, and system state. However, native GUI/code coordination cannot be obtained by prompt-level tool composition. In our preliminary experiments, naively adding a code tool degrades a GUI agent, revealing that GUI/code routing must be internalized through training on high-quality hybrid data. We present OS-Helix, an end-to-end trained multimodal computer-using agent that unifies GUI actions and code execution in one action space. To construct the required supervision, we introduce application-artifact composition, pairing desktop applications with authentic file artifacts to instantiate executable Ubuntu states, and a decoupled instruction/evaluator generation pipeline that produces environment-grounded tasks whose final states can be verified regardless of the solution modality. We cold-start the policy with SFT on filtered hybrid data and further improve it through online RL in live desktop environments. For RL, we propose Step-balanced GSPO, which aggregates importance weight by action step rather than raw assistant tokens to prevent long code actions from dominating heterogeneous-action optimization. On OSWorld-Verified, OS-Helix-27B and OS-Helix-35B-A3B achieve relative improvements of 35.0% and 33.7% over their matched Qwen3.5 hybrid baselines, while OS-Helix-27B-RL further improves by 42.9% to reach 66.44% success. Ablations provide evidence consistent with contributions from learned GUI/code coordination, scalable verifiable supervision, and action step balanced optimization, while demonstrating cross-platform transfer on WindowsAgentArena. Our project homepage is at https://os-copilot.github.io/OS-Helix/.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: MMSearch-OPD: Easy Made Hard, Hard Made Learnable for Long-Horizon Multimodal Search Agents
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Huanyao Zhang, Jiepeng Zhou, Jiaye Lin, Ontai Tang, Jingtian Hao
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: MMSearch-OPD enhances long-horizon multimodal search agents through targeted data refinement, joint reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation, improving training and performance.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Multimodal deep search is moving from short queries to long-horizon investigations that continually acquire evidence. However, training such agents remains constrained by limited challenging training questions and insufficient process feedback. We introduce MMSearch-OPD, combining controllable data refinement with joint reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD). Our Refine pipeline performs targeted expansion of reasoning chains derived from existing simple multimodal questions. Parameterized transformations control search depth and cross-modal evidence requirements while reusing existing image--question pairs. For training, answer rewards and lightweight behavior penalties guide RL, while the reward gap modulates token-level teacher guidance on imperfect student trajectories. An exponentially decaying distillation coefficient reduces teacher dependence as training proceeds. Experiments show gains from data refinement and further improvements from joint training after SFT, indicating stronger long-horizon multimodal deep search capabilities.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Tianjiao Yu, Zhilin Ou, Yifan Shen, Xinzhuo Li, Yuanzhe Liu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: CoDA is a co-evolution framework that enhances robot training by integrating simulation data engines and action policies through a shared memory of failures and learning progress, significantly improving out-of-distribution success rates.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Generative simulation can automate robot environment construction, but physically valid environments are not necessarily useful for training. The challenge is to identify environments that address a policy's failures and supervision that helps it overcome them. We introduce CoDA, a framework in which a simulation data engine and an action policy co-evolve through a shared heterogeneous memory of environment construction, policy failures, and learning progress. The memory compiles validated diagnoses from a vision-language critic into generation programs that recreate difficulties and training programs that help the policy overcome them. We further propose Text2potential to convert these diagnoses into staged potentials for action-chunk value learning, providing dense supervision for policy updates while preserving the task's optimal policy under standard shaping assumptions. Measured learning progress guides further generation and program refinement. Across four manipulation task families, CoDA improves out-of-distribution success from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6%, exceeding the strongest closed-loop baseline by 9.5 percentage points with the same generation budget. On LIBERO-Pro, 15 rounds of generation and training raise success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: UniFGVC: Universal Training-Free Few-Shot Fine-Grained Vision Classification via Attribute-Aware Multimodal Retrieval
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Haiyun Guo, Hongyu Guo, Xiangzhao Hao, Jiarui Guo, Jinqiao Wang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: UniFGVC introduces a training-free retrieval framework for few-shot fine-grained visual classification, leveraging multimodal attributes to enhance recognition without overfitting.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Few-shot fine-grained visual classification (FGVC) aims to discriminate between subtly different categories with very limited data. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLM) exhibit strong capabilities in both fine-grained visual understanding and open-world category recognition, directly fine-tuning them on few-shot FGVC tasks typically leads to overfitting on sparse samples, which erodes their valuable open-world knowledge and compromises generalization. To fundamentally overcome this limitation, we present UniFGVC, a universal training-free framework that shifts the paradigm from parameter fine-tuning to training-free retrieval-based inference. UniFGVC reframes few-shot FGVC as a multimodal retrieval problem using predefined category templates. Its core is the Category-Discriminative Visual Captioner (CDV-Captioner), an attribute-aware module designed to leverage MLLM for generating structured textual descriptions that explicitly pinpoint discriminative visual attributes between similar classes. By integrating chain-of-thought reasoning and visual references, CDV-Captioner mitigates hallucination and maximizes the discriminative power of textual captions, thereby converting images into attribute-enriched image-description pairs. Subsequently, utilizing arbitrary pre-trained visual and textual encoders in a plug-and-play manner, UniFGVC extracts features from both modalities and computes their similarity with all category templates for recognition. Extensive experiments on 12 FGVC datasets demonstrate UniFGVC's universal compatibility and consistent superiority. It not only outperforms existing few-shot CLIP-based methods but also surpasses several fully-supervised MLLM-based approaches, confirming the general advantage of the proposed retrieval paradigm.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Affordance-Aware Interactive Decision-Making and Execution for Ambiguous Instructions
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Hengxuan Xu, Fengbo Lan, Zhixin Zhao, Shengjie Wang, Mengqiao Liu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The AIDE framework enhances robot interaction with ambiguous instructions by integrating vision-language reasoning and interactive exploration, achieving high success rates in task planning and execution.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Enabling robots to explore and act in unfamiliar environments under ambiguous human instructions by interactively identifying task-relevant objects (e.g., cups or beverages for "I'm thirsty") remains challenging for existing vision-language model (VLM)-based methods, due to inefficient reasoning and limited environmental interaction. These factors hinder real-time task planning and execution. To address this, we propose Affordance-Aware Interactive Decision-Making and Execution for Ambiguous Instructions (AIDE), a human-inspired dual-stream framework that integrates interactive exploration with vision-language reasoning: mirroring the complementary deliberative and intuitive processes of human cognition, Multi-Stage Inference (MSI) serves as the decision-making stream and Accelerated Decision-Making (ADM) as the execution stream, enabling zero-shot affordance analysis and interpretation of ambiguous instructions. Experiments in simulation and real-world settings show that AIDE achieves over 80% task planning success rate and more than 95% closed-loop continuous execution accuracy at 10 Hz, surpassing existing VLM-based methods in diverse open scenarios.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: LIBERO-Industry: Benchmarking Robotic Manipulation under Industrial Process Constraints
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Ming Shin Cindy Sung, Duan Leijiahao, Haoxiang Wang, Boning Tan, Liangna Fu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: LIBERO-Industry introduces a benchmark for evaluating robotic manipulation under industrial constraints, revealing performance degradation with increasing complexity across various task scenarios.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Industrial manipulation in flexible manufacturing, e.g., high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly, requires robot policies to adapt to changing products and production conditions. Such settings impose industrial process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances. However, existing evaluation frameworks do not systematically capture these constraints when assessing generalist robot policies. To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO-Industry, a novel benchmark built on the widely used robot learning benchmark LIBERO, that translates the aforementioned industrial constraints into controllable task conditions and measurable success criteria. Specifically, LIBERO-Industry comprises three classic task scenarios: Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer. The suites contain 216 tasks in total that systematically vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and geometric acceptance region size. Extensive experiments across five generalist robot policies (including vision-language-action models and world-action models) show that performance progressively degrades as industrial constraints are introduced and combined. Under a shared fine-tuning and evaluation protocol, the LIBERO-Industry co-training condition achieved higher observed target-transfer completion than the original-LIBERO condition.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Provably Efficient Risk-Sensitive Offline Reinforcement Learning via Optimized Certainty Equivalents
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Hanzhen Wang, Boxiang Lyu, Zhongxiang Dai, Siyang Gao, Dake Zhang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: This paper presents novel offline reinforcement learning algorithms using optimized certainty equivalents, establishing theoretical bounds and addressing risk sensitivity in decision-making under uncertainty.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) addresses decision-making under uncertainty and adverse outcomes. Learning risk-sensitive policies from fixed datasets is important when additional interaction with the environment is costly. Existing work on risk-sensitive RL focuses on online settings or specific risk measures, leaving a general theoretical understanding of its offline setting underdeveloped. In this work, we investigate efficient offline risk-sensitive RL using the optimized certainty equivalent (OCE), a general class of risk measures. We consider two formulations: dynamic-OCE RL, which applies OCE recursively at each step, and static-OCE RL, which applies a single OCE to the cumulative rewards. Under the tabular setting, we develop pessimistic value-iteration algorithms for both formulations and establish tight sublinear suboptimality bounds, explicitly capturing how risk sensitivity, encoded by utility functions, affects learning difficulty. Moreover, we establish minimax suboptimality lower bounds to characterize the problem's fundamental limits. To handle large state spaces, we further develop pessimistic least-squares value-iteration algorithms that incorporate the general OCE risk criterion into linear function approximation. We establish utility-dependent sublinear guarantees with explicit dependence on the feature dimension $d$. To our knowledge, we provide the first offline algorithms along with the first upper and lower suboptimality bounds for both dynamic- and static-OCE RL.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Dual-Evolving Reinforcement Learning for Automated Reward Design
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Sitao Cheng, Tianle Li, Xuhan Huang, Xunjian Yin, Difan Zou
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: Dual-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (DERL) enhances automated reward design by using a dual-training framework that adapts reward structures based on inner policy performance feedback.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Crafting effective reward signals remains a central challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) for complex reasoning. Existing methods for automated reward optimization search with a fixed proposer which never learns from its costly trials. We present Dual-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (DERL), a dual-training framework for autonomous discovery of reward structures. An outer-loop proposer composes a reward from task primitives, and an inner policy trains with this reward. The proposer itself learns by policy gradient from the validation performance of the inner policy. Thus, DERL utilizes past-trial feedback to shape its reward-proposal distribution, an empirical meta-gradient of task success. We validate DERL on embodied (ALFWorld), scientific (ScienceWorld), and mathematical (GSM8K, MATH) reasoning. On multi-turn agent benchmarks, DERL outperforms strong baselines, significantly on out-of-distribution tasks. In mathematics, DERL improves on the outcome reward where directly added primitives hurt. Further analyses under matched compute show that our proposer effectively captures the meta-gradient to discover useful reward signals.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: VGGT-Diff: Visual Geometry Meets Diffusion for Sparse-View Novel View Synthesis
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Kangjie Chen, Xiangyu Li, Dongbin Zhang, Chaoda Zheng, Shijia Chen
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: VGGT-Diff integrates geometry-based routing with a diffusion model for enhanced novel view synthesis from sparse views, achieving state-of-the-art performance through robust conditioning and consistency techniques.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: We present VGGT-Diff, a geometry-routed multi-view diffusion model for sparse-view novel view synthesis. Existing novel view synthesis (NVS) methods face a fundamental trade-off: reconstruction-based approaches preserve observed geometry but struggle to synthesize unseen regions, while diffusion-based methods provide strong generative priors yet rely on implicit source-to-query correspondence. VGGT-Diff bridges these regimes by routing visual geometry latents from VGGT-Ω into a pretrained video diffusion model. Each visual token is associated with a 3D point and confidence, then transformed into query-aligned latent conditions through a confidence-aware Visual Geometry Router (VGR) that preserves front and back surface evidence. These conditions guide joint target-view denoising, while Point-Track Residual Consistency (PTRC) regularizes predicted-clean residuals along reliable 3D tracks, improving multi-view stability. We further introduce robust geometry conditioning, combining training-time regularization with inference-time guidance for improved robustness. Experiments show competitive or state-of-the-art performance across interpolation and extrapolation under different viewpoint difficulties. Our code is available at https://github.com/chenkangjie1123/VGGT-Diff.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Coordi-pi: Coordination-Aware Dual-Hand Action Representation for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yiming Meng, Yanming Shao, Weijie Shen, Kunyang Lin, Jiayu Sun
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: Coordi-$\pi$ introduces a structured action representation for bimanual manipulation, enhancing performance significantly by explicitly encoding hand identity and temporal synchronization.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but extending them to bimanual dexterous manipulation introduces a high-dimensional and structured action space. Existing bimanual VLA policies commonly concatenate right- and left-side arm--hand actions at each control timestep, leaving cross-hand interactions implicit within a single action vector. We introduce Coordi-$π$, a structured action representation for bimanual dexterous manipulation. Coordi-$π$ represents the right- and left-side arm--hand actions as individual action tokens and organizes them into an interleaved sequence, explicitly exposing the two sides within the action sequence. To explicitly encode hand identity and temporal synchronization in this interleaved representation, a learnable hand-identity embedding distinguishes the two sides, while sequence--control-timestep factorized rotary positional encoding (RoPE) separates sequence position from control timestep, allowing actions at the same control timestep to share a temporal coordinate while retaining distinct sequence positions. Across all five bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks in DexJoCo, Coordi-$π$ achieves state-of-the-art performance under both \textit{rand-obj} and \textit{rand-full}, improving the average success rate over $π_{0.5}$ from 31.9\% to 51.3\% and from 18.3\% to 32.3\%, respectively. Coordi-$π$ also consistently outperforms $π_{0.5}$ across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: LAGO: Language Agents with Reusable Growing Options
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yuran Wu, Mengkang Hu, Qionglin Qiu, Fanqing Meng, Qiguang Chen
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: LAGO introduces reusable language agents as temporally extended options to enhance task decomposition and execution, achieving improved performance on long-horizon tasks without model weight updates.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Long-horizon tasks expose a weakness of monolithic tool-use loops: one agent must decompose, execute, and verify a task within a single trajectory. We introduce LAGO, which treats specialized language agents as reusable temporally extended options. A meta-agent retrieves options from a persistent library or spawns new ones, dispatches sub-tasks, verifies results, and admits successful novel options. The library grows across tasks without updating model weights. On 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks, frozen Qwen3.5-35B-A3B in both roles resolves 58.6% under single-attempt evaluation with the official Docker evaluator. On a fixed 150-task subset, we re-run mini-SWE-agent, Terminus 2, and LAGO with the same policy, temperature, task IDs, and evaluator; their resolve rates are 49.3%, 57.3%, and 60.3%, respectively. Cross-model experiments provide evidence consistent with a role for decomposition quality. A 50-task component ablation finds four fewer resolved tasks without decomposition, two fewer with shuffled reused content, and six fewer without the library. These results support reusable agent-options as a practical abstraction for task streams, while leaving component-level causality task- and model-dependent.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Atomic-WAM: Execution-Grounded Atomic-Motion Reasoning for World Action Models
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Shijun Shi, Zhe Liu, Zhi Hou, Yinan Chen, Tao Zhang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: Atomic-WAM integrates task reasoning and action generation through atomic-motion descriptions, enhancing robotic control with execution-grounded learning for improved task success rates.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) typically adapt video foundation models to robotic control through joint video and action prediction. However, task-level instructions may leave the next physical interaction underspecified, requiring semantic grounding and state-dependent motion selection. To this end, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to action generation through atomic-motion descriptions. Specifically, a vision-language reasoner describes the next local motion from the task instruction and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict future video and an action chunk. Furthermore, an automatic annotation pipeline curates temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations. To make atomic-motion predictions executable by the WAM, we post-train the reasoner with Execution-Grounded GRPO (EG-GRPO). With the WAM fixed, EG-GRPO adapts the reasoner through rewards for motion appropriateness and execution success. Finally, Atomic-WAM achieves 39.6% task success under default instructions and 31.6% under vague instructions in a real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab. Project page: https://ssj9596.github.io/Atomic-WAM-project

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Reflect After Failure: Brain-Inspired Self-Evolving Agents for Embodied Spatial Intelligence
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Xin Li, Xiaohuan Gu, Yifan Wang, Shaobin Ling, Tianli Shi
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: HiMeco, a brain-inspired self-evolving agent, enhances embodied spatial intelligence by diagnosing failures and refining strategies through metacognitive reflection and memory consolidation.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have made substantial progress in spatial reasoning, and self-evolving agents further extend these capabilities to embodied environments by learning from interactions. However, current self-evolution remains particularly challenging in embodied spatial tasks, complex and multi-step decisions from partial visual evidence making it difficult to determine why an execution fails. The failure may stem from misperception, insufficient exploration, or incorrect planning, yet execution feedback alone rarely reveals which component is responsible. As a result, simply accumulating interaction experience can reinforce ineffective strategies. To address this, we propose HiMeco, a brain-inspired self-evolving agent for embodied spatial intelligence, inspired by metacognitive monitoring and hippocampal memory consolidation. Through Hippocampal-Metacognitive Reflection, HiMeco diagnoses failures in perception-exploration-planning (PEP), then compares execution attempts to derive reusable strategies and guidance for avoiding recurring errors. It also abstracts interaction programs into parameterized skills, using evidence contracts and execution-based validation to determine their retention and reuse. These strategies and skills guide subsequent interactions, with memory updated only between rounds and model parameters kept frozen. HiMeco achieves state-of-the-art performance on ESI-Bench, and it also improves accuracy on EmbSpatial-Bench by 3.94 percentage points without evolution.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: PingpongDuo: Agile Humanoid Table Tennis Doubles with Safe Team Coordination
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Haoran Jiang, Yichao Zhong, Kai Zhang, Cheng Liu, Yixuan Pan
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: PingpongDuo is a hierarchical framework enabling agile humanoid table tennis doubles with safe coordination, improving ball-return success by 13.2% and achieving rapid, precise movements.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Unlike singles, humanoid table tennis doubles requires teammates to strike in strict alternation while sharing a confined workspace. Rapid repositioning can compromise striking accuracy, while uncoordinated teammate movements introduce collision risks. We present PingpongDuo, a hierarchical framework for agile humanoid doubles with safe team coordination. At the team level, a planner jointly selects positioning targets and uses learned risk estimates to filter risky proposals, preferentially preserving the current striker's target. At the individual level, separate footwork and striking skills combine agile movement with precise racket control. The skills are guided by human motion references, including footwork collected from human doubles play, and trained from states produced by one another to support rapid transitions. A racket-arm residual further refines strikes after movement using return feedback from a simulator calibrated with real ball-flight and contact measurements. In simulation, PingpongDuo improves the ball-return success rate by 13.2% over the state-of-the-art baseline, while achieving approximately 2 cm positioning error during clearance. In real-world experiments, a robot completes a 2.15 m clearance-and-recovery cycle in 2.4 s with a peak speed of 2.23 m/s, while two robots sustain more than 10 consecutive strikes in strict alternation.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: REVEAL: Reverse Engineering Agentic Latents from Frontier-Model Traces
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yuetian Du, Meng Wang, Yucheng Wang, Zhangzhe Chen, Wei Wang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The REVEAL framework enables the extraction of reusable local controls from frontier-model trajectories, enhancing smaller agents' performance without requiring model retraining.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Frontier LLM agents perform complex interactive tasks, but their inference costs motivate transferring their experience to smaller open-source agents. Distillation and latent communication typically require target-model training or access to source-model internals. We study how textual frontier-model trajectories can provide reusable local controls for a frozen agent. Inspired by protocol reverse engineering, we introduce $\textit{Agentic Latents}$, comprising anchored states and dynamic profiles of feedback--response cycles elicited by replay in the target model. Our training-free framework, $\textbf{REVEAL}$ ($\textbf{REV}$erse $\textbf{E}$ngineering $\textbf{A}$gentic $\textbf{L}$atents), uses these profiles and trajectory outcomes to match and select local events from successful and failed rollouts of the same task and source model. Their response-transition contrasts yield a target-specific steering direction, applied before each response. Within-benchmark evaluations on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and Humanity's Last Exam with tools report higher accuracy than unmodified agents across three targets. Representation analyses and behavioral case studies support reusing frontier-model experience as local activation control.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: DiffGIPC: Differentiable Mixed-Coordinate Contact Dynamics on GPU
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Kemeng Huang, Bowen Ren, Xinyu Lu, Minchen Li, Taku komura
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: DiffGIPC is a GPU-accelerated framework that efficiently optimizes contact-rich dynamics in deformable and rigid bodies, achieving significant speedups in gradient evaluations while ensuring non-penetration.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Contact-rich inverse problems require efficient gradients and reliable enforcement of non-penetration. Existing differentiable methods provide fast simulation and rigid-deformable coupling, but contact treatments based on penalties or velocity-level constraints can permit penetration or positional drift. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) maintains non-penetration through geometric barriers and {continuous collision detection (CCD)}. However, repeated forward and backward evaluations remain costly in full-space finite-element (FEM) implementations, particularly when nearly rigid components retain many vertex {degrees of freedom (DoFs)}. We present DiffGIPC, a GPU-accelerated differentiable IPC framework for optimizing interacting deformable and nearly rigid bodies. Our affine-body derivatives enable {rest-shape} design, initial-state optimization, and articulated control while retaining only twelve motion DoFs per affine body. These gradients account for how changes in geometry, placement, and actuation affect other objects through collision and friction. We preserve these interactions in one coupled FEM-affine adjoint system per frame, reducing the backward-system size without discarding the dependencies that drive the inverse problem. GPU-optimized backward computation further reduces the cost of repeated gradient evaluations. A reusable PyTorch interface connects supported physical parameters to user-defined parameter maps and losses across design, identification, motion, placement, and articulated control. Experiments demonstrate peak speedups over DiffIPC of approximately 150.0x with full-space FEM and 4133.3x with affine bodies for combined forward simulation and backward differentiation.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: EvoWeave: Composing Reusable Agent Experience through Operation Level Graphs
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Guanhua Zhu, Bo Shen, Lei Zhang, Fadi Deek, Zhi Wei
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: EvoWeave is a framework that enhances interactive agents' task performance by efficiently composing reusable operations through a structured experience memory and dependency graph.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Different tasks often require interactive agents to perform similar operations at intermediate steps. Retrieving an entire past workflow can introduce irrelevant steps, whereas retrieving isolated operations can discard the dependencies needed to reuse them. We introduce EvoWeave, a framework for experience memory that represents abstract states as nodes and reusable operations as directed edges with input and output contracts, provenance, and capability references. A planner decomposes the current task into a dependency graph; operation retrieval and bounded directed search then assemble relevant experience fragments. An execution agent can inspect these fragments and their referenced capabilities, while reflection separates concrete execution evidence from reusable abstractions. We study the framework across four benchmarks, five evaluation settings, and three language model backbones. Across backbones, AppWorld Normal and Challenge task goal completion average 51.91 and 27.99, respectively, exceeding the baseline without memory by 6.99 and 4.99 percentage points. An AppWorld ablation associates directed connections with an additional improvement of 2.08 points over independent operation cards. The results motivate composition of reusable operations while exposing tradeoffs in retrieval overhead and conditions for valid reuse.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: FOMI: A Force-Feedback Manipulation Interface for Teaching Contact-Rich Manipulation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yishu Shen, Yiming Luo, Ruilin Wang, Bowen Yang, Shuai Yang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: FOMI is a novel force-feedback interface that enhances robot-free collection of contact-rich demonstrations, improving efficiency and enabling effective teleoperation for manipulation tasks.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Robot-free collection with handheld interfaces enables scalable acquisition of human demonstrations for policy learning. However, existing handheld interfaces often provide limited intuitive force feedback, making contact-rich demonstration collection challenging for human operators. To address this, we present FOMI, a force-feedback manipulation interface with a scissor-shaped mechanism, which transmits object interaction forces directly to the operator's hands through actuation links without force sensors. This intuitive force feedback supports real-time action adjustment during robot-free collection of contact-rich demonstrations. Around FOMI, we build a demonstration collection system that integrates sensor calibration, data acquisition, and synchronization for robot-free collection. By further mapping pose changes and gripper opening of FOMI to robot end-effector poses and gripper commands, the system also supports teleoperation. Across four contact-rich tasks, FOMI improves collection efficiency by approximately 29% and 18% over the best baselines in robot-free collection and teleoperation, respectively. Demonstrations collected with FOMI in both modes enable policies to perform challenging contact-rich manipulation tasks with high success rates.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Designing Textual Interfaces To Enhance Llm Reasoning On Audio-Visual Question Answering
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yi Wang, Tianzi Wang, Tong Lei, Dahan Wang, Peter Bell
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: This paper explores how different textual interface designs impact prompt optimization for audio-visual question answering in multimodal reasoning systems, revealing trade-offs in interpretability and optimization difficulty.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) has shown strong effectiveness for text-based LLMs and LLM systems, but its application to audio-visual understanding systems requires suitable textual interfaces through which multimodal reasoning can be exposed to text-based optimizers. We investigate how the design of textual interfaces affects prompt optimization for multimodal reasoning, on the audio-visual question answering task. We compare three interface designs, including a direct inference system consisting of a single omni-modal large language model (OmniLLM), a captioner-reasoner system, and an agentic architecture in which a primary agent orchestrates subagent OmniLLMs. Experiments with Qwen3-Omni and Gemini show that direct prompt optimization provides model-dependent gains; the captioner-reasoner system and the agentic system expose more interpretable optimization interfaces but are harder to optimize, where error analysis of cases affected by optimization is conducted. Our study highlights textual interface design as an important factor in making prompt optimization effective for omni-modal reasoning systems. Our implementation details are specified in GitHub repo.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Towards Agentic Robots: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Chonghan Qin, Dongming Wu, Kaituo Feng, Jiaxu Wang, Xinlei Yu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: This paper outlines the evolving concept of agentic robots, categorizing research into four domains while addressing challenges and future directions for enhancing robotic intelligence and adaptability.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Foundation models are driving a paradigm shift in robotic intelligence, moving beyond low-level action prediction to goal-directed orchestration of data collection, model training, task planning, and real-world execution. We characterize this emerging paradigm as an agentic robots, in which agents reason over human instructions, interact with robotic environments, rectify execution errors autonomously, and dynamically adjust operational strategies. Although this field develops fast, current studies are not well connected. Researchers have no consistent view of how to combine different agentic functions into a complete robot system. This paper provides a unified overview of existing research on agentic robots. We first trace the development from robot policies to agentic systems, covering vision-language-action models, world models, and world-action models. We then clarify the definition and scope of agentic robots and organize existing research into seventeen categories across four functional domains: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness. Across these domains, we examine how agents shape model learning and robot decisions, collect and curate robot data, construct worlds, tasks, and tests for learning and evaluation, and organize capabilities for robot use. Finally, we discuss open challenges and outline directions for future research. Looking forward, we hope this work contributes to a clearer understanding of agentic robots and supports new approaches to making them more capable, reliable, and adaptive.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: KineWorld: Action-Induced Transport Fields for Embodied World Modeling
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Ziying Song, Yuchen Liu, Zhuoran Xu, Ziyang Liu, Jian Jin
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: KineWorld introduces a transport-aware framework for embodied world modeling, enhancing action prediction by aligning visual generation with critical spatial changes in robot interactions.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Embodied world models predict the visual consequences of candidate actions before execution. However, existing action-conditioned world models often adopt uniformly weighted visual generation objectives that can be misaligned with embodied prediction needs. Even with explicit motion conditioning, these objectives can underemphasize spatially sparse changes that are critical to interaction. We propose KineWorld, a transport-aware world-modeling framework that extends robot kinematics from motion conditioning to the spatial allocation of generative supervision. Kinematic Transport Lifting (KTL) constructs renderer-derived, camera-aligned transport fields from commanded robot motion. Transport-Aware World Diffusion (TAWD) calibrates their motion support on the video-latent grid and reweights future-RGB flow matching through a normalized mixture of uniform and transport-focused distributions. We train KineWorld using ALOHA-AgileX bimanual manipulation data from RoboTwin 2.0. KineWorld achieves an EWMScore-P of 68.95 in single-view evaluation and a TWB-Score of 54.82 in multi-view evaluation. These results support a shift from appearance fitting toward action-consequence modeling for embodied decision-making.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: MathVis: Can AI Reason through Drawing? A Benchmark for Mathematical Figure Generation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Jingjing Wei, Hao Zhao, Xinke Li, Linxi Yu, Xiaosong Gao
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The MathVis benchmark evaluates LLMs' diagram-assisted reasoning in math problem visualization, revealing limitations in their ability to produce clear, visually coherent outputs.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: This paper introduces MathVis, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' ability to visualize frontier mathematical problems and perform diagram-assisted reasoning. The benchmark consists of 512 tasks, each comprising a mathematical statement, a reference diagram, executable TikZ or SVG code, a Gold Intermediate Representation (IR), atomic rubrics, and error codes. Through rigorous evaluation, GPT-6-Astra, Claude Fable 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve pass@1 scores of 31.25%, 26.56%, and 22.85%, respectively. We found that although the tasks require visualization, LLMs produce outputs dominated by formal languages, symbols, and graphics programs, rather than explicit diagram-mediated reasoning. Furthermore, while the solutions generated by LLMs may contain all the necessary elements, they are often visually confusing to humans. Ultimately, this benchmark aims to visualize mathematical problems and promote research on enabling LLMs to simplify their reasoning via visual diagrams.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: ReAT: Residual Action Tokenization for Autoregressive Robot Policies
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Dijia Zhan, Zhuo Li, Xuemiao Xu, Sun Zheng, Jinyi Li
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper presents Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), enhancing autoregressive robot policies by enabling tokens to iteratively refine action reconstructions, improving performance across various tasks.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Autoregressive robot policies rely on action tokenizers to convert continuous action chunks into compact sequences of discrete prediction targets. Existing tokenizers can reconstruct action chunks from discrete codes, but often leave implicit what each individual token contributes to the reconstructed action. We introduce Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), which gives each token an explicit role in refining the current action reconstruction.
